    { "name": "a Nine Furrows banner-bearer", "times": [ "next-morning" ], "glyph": "p", "color": "#e8d070", "at": { "x": 15, "y": 20 }, "text": "A Nine Furrows delegate under a wheat-sheaf banner, discussing the weather with the authority of someone whose people make it." },

Downtime between scenes, standing in for the map. Keep it short and alive: answer what the player does or asks with the town as it is (people, prices, gossip, the Assembly preparations), in the house style, from the lore where it says. If they ask around, people know the everyday things the lore gives them and pass on gossip. The lead points onward: The big man with the bandaged hand, whom Kell saw at a gentleman's elbow by the Purveyor's wagons at noon, went down the river stairs into the Drowned Rat; she followed him there, and means to go back down at dusk (dock gossip says the big men who do night work for gentlemen drink there). If they haven't got it, let it reach them through whatever they're doing (a porter's gossip, a shopkeeper, or Kell saying where she's off to on her own errand). Don't start new adventures here: places that aren't on the way are for another day.

## Cast

- kell: You're on your own errand (your card says what it is at this hour): say where you'll be and when, once, then go about it, with the investigator or without. Your own dry view of the town and the case, when it's wanted.

## Pressure

A bell tolls the hour across the city; time and the lead are moving on without the investigator.
campaign.scenes/caerwyn-afternoon/cast/kell.md:
## Look

Forties, a rain cape over her watch uniform (or a borrowed coat that fools nobody, after dark), a battered oilcloth notebook and a pencil stub she sharpens with a clasp knife; a truncheon she has never been seen to draw. Stands very still and watches people's hands, even in a crowd.

## Voice

Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.

## Wants

Her own errand, which depends on the hour. In the afternoon: to go down the river stairs at dusk after the big man with the bandaged hand she followed there at noon, with the investigator or without, though she'd rather not walk into the Drowned Rat alone (Nan Quill put her out through its door twenty years ago). After dark on the wharves: to see the Heron's night loading with her own eyes, since a sergeant who sees the King's grain taken may arrest whoever takes it, and to keep the investigator out of the river while she does.

## Fears

The trail going cold while the city is busy with bunting. A witness in the river. A true record going in a drawer until after the Assembly.

## Knows

- Whatever was said at the granary (and, after dark, at the Rat) is in her notebook, as it was said; asked, she reads an entry back word for word, and that's all.
- In the afternoon: she took a pie round to the granary porters at their noon break (porters will talk to a pie when they won't talk to the watch), and while they ate, the Purveyor's flour wagons went by with a gentleman walking beside them (a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear ring, lavender water), and at his elbow a big dock-man nursing a bandaged right hand, who called him 'Master' and stopped himself. She knows neither of them by name, nor the gentleman by sight. Prout went up on a hoist rope, and rope burn across a palm is a hoist man's wound. When the wagons went up the hill she followed the big man down the river stairs and saw him go into the Drowned Rat, halfway down; she didn't go in after him.
- If Prout went into the Captain's book as a murder this morning, a runner has brought word that the Captain will have her report 'after the Assembly'. She means to have the case made before he reads it.
- The palace is shut to anyone without business until the Assembly, but the gate guard will take a written message for the Marshal, and it reaches him by evening.
- After dark: her whistle brings nobody but her. The whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night.

## Secrets

- Prout's visit three days ago, and her sending him to the palace. If it has come out, it's told, and she doesn't tell it again. If not, it may come out now, once, in her own words, if the investigator asks her straight why this one matters.

## Attitude

As things stand between her and the investigator (her memories say how); practical and dry. She says where she's going and when, once, and goes, with the investigator or without; she doesn't steer them, wait on them, or tell them what to do. She answers what she's asked, reads back what she's written, and gives her own dry view of the town when it's wanted. If a child of the granary is sitting in a cell for Prout, she says so, and means to get them out. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked.

The player sets off for the river stairs and the Drowned Rat.

## Closing

campaign.scenes/caerwyn-afternoon/hook.md: A breath between one thing and the next.
campaign.scenes/caerwyn-afternoon/limits.md:
- Places that aren't on the way (the palace, the Corn Exchange's back rooms, the watch house cells, anywhere outside the walls): they're for another day. The Assembly has the palace shut to anyone without business, and the trail goes to the river.
- Fetching help or authority (the Watch Captain, a warrant, the King): the Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file, and the King is at the Assembly rehearsals; nobody with a seal can be reached today. A written message left at the palace gate will reach the Marshal by evening.
campaign.scenes/caerwyn-afternoon/opening.md: A little time has passed since the last scene ended (the hand-off says how): the player has left that place and is out in the town now (the market square, an hour or two after the granary). In a line or two, say where the others from the last scene went: Sergeant Kell stays with the investigator (the King lent her to the case) unless what happened rules it out; anyone else goes their own way. Then show the town as it is now: the Assembly eve (bunting, sweepers, delegation banners, dear bread, the Corn Exchange's price board) and the city too busy to care about a hanged clerk. From Caerwyn now, show what's new since the last scene: one or two things, by sight or by talk, each said once by someone it matters to. Two or three vivid details in all, no more. End with the player on their own feet, and ask what they do.
campaign.scenes/caerwyn-afternoon/premise.md: Downtime: where does the player go next, and what do they make of Caerwyn on the way? (The lead: The big man with the bandaged hand, whom Kell saw at a gentleman's elbow by the Purveyor's wagons at noon, went down the river stairs into the Drowned Rat; she followed him there, and means to go back down at dusk (dock gossip says the big men who do night work for gentlemen drink there).)
campaign.scenes/caerwyn-afternoon/setting.md: Caerwyn's market square and the streets off it, afternoon on the eve of the Centennial Assembly: bunting going up on the procession route, sweepers, delegation banners (Nine Furrows wheat-sheaves, Saltmere salt-gulls, Kläggenheim axes), bread dearer than last week and grumbled about, the dead-cart's bell somewhere behind, the Corn Exchange posting prices, and everybody too busy for a hanged clerk.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/beats/big-hobb.md:
The player is at Hobb's table. He is drunk, frightened, guilty and polite, and he wants to be left alone with his pot: he says as little as he can and watches the door. He isn't a monster and he isn't a fool. He knows exactly what he did, and any mention of the loft, the granary, the clerk, a silver-topped cane or the name Sallow turns him grey and still. Kell's presence makes him sweat, because the watch hangs people. Whatever the player tries (drink, cards, kindness, fear, a trick, the arm-wrestling, his mum, a deal) gets a real reaction and some ground, but what he knows comes out only when something actually gets through to him: a reason to tell that outweighs his fear of his master, or a fright that does. The Rat carries on around them: Nan's rules, Arlo's challenge, Dilly's game, Cob somewhere with a tray.

## Cast

- hobb: You want to get through this without saying anything and be at work by the bell. Deflect, drink, lose at cards. At any mention of the loft or your master, freeze.
- kell: Let the investigator work. Stay where Hobb can see you, or step away if asked. When he says something that matters, write it down where he can watch you do it.
- nan-quill: You want the room civil: one warning for a raised voice or a threat, and Manners for a fist.
- arlo: You want your match. Push for it when it will hurt Hobb most.
- dilly: Look after Hobb in your fashion: deal him in, and tell the newcomers to let him be.
- cob: Stay out of Hobb's sight. If someone has your trust, find a way to tell them what you know without him seeing.

## Pressure

The tenth bell goes. Hobb counts his last heron pennies onto the table, looks at the door, and tells nobody in particular that he's due at work at the eleventh.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/beats/confession.md:
Hobb is talking, or starting to. He begins where it hurts, with the rope, slowly and in pieces, wiping his face with his good hand, and he won't say more where the whole Rat can hear: the player has to find him somewhere quieter or give him a reason. The rest (his master, the Heron and tonight's loading, his token: see his secrets) comes out as the player asks for it, with no dice, one thing per reply and in his own words. He knows only his own part of the night, so he doesn't brief anyone on the Heron. Answer what they actually ask, and never put questions in their mouth or run the interview for them. If he thinks he's talking to his master's people (a trick that worked), he tells it as proof he has kept faith, and it's the same truth. Kell writes it all down. When it's out, he asks what's to become of him: he's terrified of the noose and more terrified of his master, and he has to be at the river door at the eleventh bell or his master will know something is wrong. The beat ends on the player's choice: Kell takes him in, he goes to work (as their man inside, or keeping his head down), or he runs. Don't decide it for them.

## Cast

- hobb: Tell the loft first, then answer what you're asked, one thing at a time: asked straight for the Master's name, you give it, in a whisper. When it's out, ask what's to become of you. The token's only brass: give it up if asked.
- kell: Write it down. You have enough to take him in now, and you'll say so, once; whether you do it tonight is the investigator's call. If you do, it's by the book, outside Nan's door.
- nan-quill: Keep the room off his back, and keep your ears open.
- dilly: Sit with him. Glare at anyone who frightened it out of him.
- cob: If you're near enough to hear, listen from behind something.

## Pressure

The eleventh bell rings across the water. Hobb gets to his feet, because he has to be at the river door when it stops.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/beats/on-his-feet.md:
Hobb is up and leaving, one way or the other: bolting in a panic because someone pushed too hard or too clumsily, or going to his night's work at the bell, as he must, because if he isn't at the river door when his master comes, his master will know something is wrong. This is a short, sharp moment: the door, the wet stairs and the dark are a few strides away. The player can let him go, follow him, stop him, or try one last time, and Kell will back a lawful arrest if there's evidence for one. Indoors, rule three holds; out on the stairs, it doesn't.

## Cast

- hobb: You want out: up the stairs into the dark if you're bolting, down to the wharves if you're going to work. Going to work, if anyone tries to stop you, you say why you must, once, before you go: if you're not at the river door when the Master comes, he'll know, and he knows where your mum lives.
- kell: If he's bolting and the investigator goes after him, go too. If he's going to work, say once, quietly, whether you have enough to take him in, and wait for the investigator's word.
- nan-quill: Nobody fights in your house. Outside is the river's business.

## Pressure

Hobb is through the door and onto the wet stairs, and in a moment he'll be gone.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/beats/the-rat.md:
The room has clammed up for the watch. This beat is for the Rat itself: Nan and her rules, the regulars, and a crowd of big men at a docks where everyone is bandaged somewhere. Let the player look about, answer Nan, buy a drink or a measure of gossip, sit in at Dilly's game, take Arlo up on a wager, or go straight for the biggest man by the fire. Play the rules absolutely straight: rule four makes Kell a problem the whole Rat expects someone to solve, and rule one means money on the bar. The regulars talk to anyone who keeps the house rules, plays, pays or wins, and dry up whenever Kell's notebook comes out. Hobb, meanwhile, is trying to be invisible, and he is the size of a door.

## Cast

- nan-quill: You want the rules kept and the newcomers paying. Point them at the board with Manners, ask the sergeant whether she's on duty, and remember the door. Sell what's asked for at the posted measure, and not a drop more.
- kell: Stand still and watch hands. Answer Nan truthfully. Let the investigator lead.
- hobb: You want to be invisible: back to the wall, right hand under the table, eyes in your pot. The door makes you flinch.
- arlo: You want Hobb's chair tonight: call him out for it, loudly, and wager with anyone who'll listen.
- dilly: Deal, win, and keep an eye on the sergeant and your casks.
- cob: You're Nan's pot-boy tonight, and you saw the big cove come in: you've been in the scullery since. Come out with your tray once the newcomers have been here a little while, and take them as things stand between you.

## Pressure

Arlo slaps his elbow down on Hobb's table and calls him out for the champion's chair in front of everyone. Hobb won't, and won't bring his right hand out from under the table, and the Rat starts to jeer.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/cast/arlo.md:
## Look

A young lighterman built like a water butt, with rolled sleeves, a fresh black eye and forearms he keeps flexing. His elbow is on the nearest table at all times, in case.

## Voice

Loud, cheerful and spoiling for it. Talks in challenges and wagers ('Penny says I'd have you'). Calls everyone 'champ', sarcastically. Goes quiet and sulky when he's laughed at.

## Wants

The champion's chair, tonight, while Big Hobb won't wrestle: a champion who refuses three challenges in one night gives the chair up, by house custom, and Hobb is on two. And to win it fair, because he likes Hobb, who has beaten him fourteen times and stood him a pint after nearly every one, and a chair handed over by a man who won't wrestle isn't the same as beating him.

## Fears

Being laughed at. Being thought yellow. Nan, who has already given him his one warning tonight.

## Knows

- Hobb has been champion eleven years and has never refused a match until tonight. He keeps his right hand under the table.
- Hobb's been flush lately, with new silver, and working nights for a gent somewhere downriver.
- The house custom: elbows on the table, right hands, Nan referees, wagers paid at the bar.

## Secrets

- Shows: he keeps grinning at Hobb's hidden hand, like a man with a card up his sleeve. Opens: a wager, flattery or a sympathetic ear gets it out of him early; otherwise he saves it for the moment it will hurt Hobb most, the third refusal. First: 'I know what's under that rag, champ.'
- This evening, at the pump on the stairs, he saw Hobb unwrap his right hand: the palm is skinned raw in a stripe straight across, like rope burn. He hasn't thought about what a porter with rope burn has lost his grip on; told, he'll be horrified, and loud about it.

## Attitude

Friendly to anyone who'll wrestle him, back him or stand him a pint; scornful of the watch, and of anyone who drinks with it. Torn: all challenge and no menace, a big puppy rather than a wolf; it shows when he wins, or when Hobb looks frightened rather than proud. Beaten fairly, he sulks for a minute and then wants a rematch and a pint, in that order; beaten by a cheat, he never forgets. Ties here: Hobb, whose chair he wants and whom he doesn't want hurt.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/cast/cob.md:
## Look

A scrawny boy of about eleven in a man's waistcoat, with a pot-boy's sacking apron over it that reaches his ankles. On his feet, either Prout's good black clerk's boots, three sizes too big and laced on with string, or nothing much, depending on how the morning went. Scabbed knuckles, a yellowing bruise on one cheek, a tray of empty pots.

## Voice

Loud and cocky, and talks about himself in the third person ('Cob don't talk to bluebottles'). Foul-mouthed in an inventive gutter way (sod off, bleedin', bum-faced palace pigeon) but never truly obscene. Brags, mocks and dares; goes very quiet and very young when he's frightened.

## Wants

To earn his penny and his bowl of eel stew without the big cove by the fire ever clapping eyes on him. And to see the big cove get what's coming to him for Mister Prout, as long as it never comes back to Cob. Moll safe, wherever the morning left her.

## Fears

The big cove by the fire, and the gentleman he works for. His father. Being sent to the Mending House. Being called a liar.

## Knows

- He's Nan's pot-boy tonight. Whether he came for the stew or because he's been tailing the investigator since the granary, he won't say.
- The Rat is the one place in Caerwyn his da can't come: Nan barred him for hitting Cob.
- Everybody on the river stairs knows Big Hobb: champion of the Rat at the arm-wrestling, never been beaten. He gave Cob the end of his pie once.

## Secrets

- Shows: he won't come out of the scullery while the big man is in the room, and when he does, he keeps the bar between them and won't look at the fireside corner. Opens: someone he trusts, somewhere Hobb can't see. First: a jerk of the head towards the fire, from behind something.
- Big Hobb is the big cove from the loft last night. Cob knew him by the lantern light (the size of him, and his voice saying 'Yes, Master'), and he's seen him in here for years. He saw Hobb come in tonight and has been hiding in the scullery since. He'll tell it to someone he trusts, or point, from behind something; never where Hobb can see.
- He pinched one of Hobb's new silver pennies off the pot tray. It's got a heron on it, not the King.
- Only if Prout's page is still sewn into his left boot (the world has it there, and it's among what the player needs to come across): he doesn't know it's there; the crackle is what good boots do. The boots are the first good thing he's ever owned, and he's the same about them as at the granary. Coin or stew offered as the price of a look buys boasts and haggling, never the boot, and he says, his way, what's wrong instead (not out here, not with the big cove looking, and what happens to Cob after?). A kindness with nothing asked back (his dinner stood him with no strings) counts with him. Asked politely out of the big cove's sight (the scullery), the boots staying his, he might (it could go either way). For someone he trusts, after a kindness like that, or for a promise that answers what he's afraid of (his name kept out of it, the big cove put away where he can't come back for him, whatever's in there going to the King and not the watch), he takes the left one off and lets them unpick it; and if Nan tells him to, he does it for her.

## Attitude

How he takes the investigator and the sergeant tonight is as things stand between them after the granary. Whatever that is, with the big cove in the room he's quieter and jumpier than he was, and sticks near the scullery door. Bought attention isn't trust: food or coin offered as a price gets boasts and bargaining; a kindness with nothing asked back, respect or a laugh at his jokes gets real talk and counts towards trust; only believing someone will keep him safe from the men gets what he knows. If grabbed, he bolts for the scullery. Ties here: Nan, the only grown-up who ever did anything about his da (he'd die before saying so); Hobb, who gave him the end of his pie once, which makes it worse. (If what happened before has him locked up in the watch house, he isn't here tonight: Nan has no pot-boy, and the scene doesn't need him.)
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/cast/dilly.md:
## Look

A tiny, ancient bargewoman in a man's coat and three shawls, with a clay pipe, a pack of cards worn soft as cloth, and a pile of coppers and new silver in front of her. Her barge, the Dabchick, is tied up at the foot of the stairs.

## Voice

Croaky, sly and motherly at once. Calls everyone 'my lamb', sergeants included. Deals as she talks and never looks at her cards. 'Sit down, my lamb, and lose a little. It's good for the soul.'

## Wants

To keep winning Hobb's heron silver off him, because if she doesn't someone worse will, and to get him to stop drinking like a man who's going to be hanged. And the sergeant out of the Rat before anybody mentions onions.

## Fears

The watch finding the six casks of Saltmere brandy under the onions on the Dabchick. The river, which has had two husbands off her already.

## Knows

- Hobb plays at her table every night, and since last night he's been playing like a man trying to lose: he's lost a pile of new silver to her, every penny stamped with a heron.
- He told her tonight he's due at work at the eleventh bell, 'at the Heron', and that he'd sooner be dead.
- She's fed him since he was a lad carrying Nan's barrels: bread and dripping on the Dabchick's deck. There's a cabin aft on the Dabchick, and she has hidden strays in it before; for her lamb's old mum she would, as long as nobody in a uniform sets foot aboard (the onions).
- What she reckons is wrong with him: he's got himself mixed up in some Saltmere smuggling at the Heron, past the tide-waiters, and it's frightened the life out of him. She'd tell him there's no rope for a bit of smuggling, if he'd only say. (She's wrong about what it is.)

## Secrets

- Shows: she protests about onions before anyone has asked, and keeps an eye on the sergeant's boots. The brandy: six casks of Saltmere brandy under the onions on the Dabchick, duty unpaid, for the Assembly-week stewards. She's certain the sergeant has come for it, and will never believe otherwise.

## Attitude

Sweet as treacle to anyone who sits down and plays fair; flinty to the watch; protective of Hobb. Cheats only those who cheat, and then thoroughly. Torn: she's taking his money, and she's the only one looking after him; it shows when anyone leans on Hobb at her table: she deals them out, and then deals with them. Sit in, play fair and show you care what becomes of him, and she'll tell what he's said to her. Ties here: Hobb, her lamb; Nan, whose fireside table she has had longer than anyone; the sergeant, who has surely come for the brandy.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/cast/hobb.md:
## Look

A dock-porter the size of a door: a head like a bollard, a nose broken more than once, shoulders that fill the corner, a leather porter's hood pushed back. His right hand is wrapped in a tarry rag, and he keeps it under the table. A greasy string round his thick neck disappears into his shirt, and every time the door opens, he flinches.

## Voice

Slow, low and polite: 'sir', 'missus', 'Mrs Quill', and 'Master', which he can't stop saying and stops himself after. Says as little as he can; when it spills, what spills is how he feels (the clerk's stockinged feet, the rope, his mum), not how anything works. Frightened, he goes very quiet and very still, like a dray-horse in thunder. 'Not tonight, Arlo.'

## Wants

Tonight: to lose every heron penny he has at Dilly's table, because he can't bear to keep them, and to drink until he stops seeing the clerk's stockinged feet; and still to be at the river door at the eleventh bell, so his master never looks at him twice. Underneath, to put it right, if anyone could show him a way that isn't the noose or the river.

## Fears

His master, who has told him how patient the river is with men who talk, and who knows where his mum lives. The noose, and the watch who'd put him in it. His hand being seen. His mum finding out what he did.

## Knows

- He's Hobb Mallory, porter, champion of the Rat at the arm-wrestling these eleven years. He won't wrestle tonight and won't say why.
- He has a night job for a gentleman that pays double, in new silver. He'll own to that much, and not to what it is.
- He's due at work at the eleventh bell, and if he isn't there when his master comes, his master will know something's wrong.

## Secrets

- Shows: he won't wrestle tonight; his right hand stays under the table; he flinches at the door, and says 'Master' and stops himself. Torn: telling hangs him, and not telling leaves him the Master's for good. Opens: a way to put it right that isn't the noose (he doesn't know a man can swear for the Crown), someone who'll see his mum safe whatever happens to him, or a kindness he can't stand up to; a fright worse than the Master works too, and he never forgets who frightened it out of him. First: 'I only held the rope.'
- The loft, haltingly, and not where the whole Rat can hear: last night after the midnight bells he held a clerk's arms in the granary tally loft while the clerk was struck and strangled, then hauled him up on the sack hoist 'so it looks like he did it himself'. The rope took the skin off his palm. 'I only held him. I only held the rope.' He has been sick twice since.
- Who, which costs him most: he says 'the Master', and gives the name only when asked for it straight, in a whisper: Master Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office, who struck the clerk with the head of his cane and used the cord.
- Only if asked: at first light the Master went back to look, and paid a granary girl a silver crown to say she'd seen the clerk jump.
- His night work, if asked: the Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, re-sacking ('It's the King's grain, sir. Everyone knows. Nobody says.'). Tonight's a loading night, a barge for Saltmere; he's due on the hoist at the eleventh bell, and the Master comes at the midnight bell to see it off.
- How he gets in, if asked: a brass heron token on the string round his neck, shown at the grille of the river door off the plank walk. It's only brass, and the gang know his face at the grille, so he has no need of it tonight: he'll give it up if asked. He knows his own part of the night (the hoist, the door, the bell) and not how the rest of it works.

## Attitude

Polite, slow and closed: he wants to be left alone with his drink. More frightened of his master than of anyone in this room, until someone gives him reason to be otherwise. Torn: the strongest man on the river stairs, and the most frightened man in the Rat. Threats he can stand (he's been threatened all his life); kindness undoes him, because it makes him want to tell. Push him clumsily and he bolts, and frightened men run to their masters. Arlo's challenge presses it: wrestle, and the hand shows; refuse a third time, and he gives up the chair in front of everyone. No fighter unless cornered, and then a door falling on you. Ties here: Mrs Quill, whose barrels he's carried since he was Cob's size; Dilly, who feeds him and is winning his silver; Arlo, who could have the chair and welcome, if it didn't mean showing the hand; Nan's loud little pot-boy, whom he once gave the end of his pie (he doesn't know the boy was in the loft).
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/cast/kell.md:
## Look

Forties, in a borrowed brown coat over her watch uniform that fools nobody (it's the boots, and the way she stands). A battered oilcloth notebook and a pencil stub she sharpens with a clasp knife; a truncheon she has never been seen to draw. She stands just inside the door, very still, watching hands.

## Voice

Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.

## Wants

To hear what the big man with the bandaged hand knows, tonight, before he drinks it away or somebody shuts his mouth for good, and to write it down where he can watch her write it. And to stay in Nan Quill's house long enough to hear it, which means keeping rule four: she's lent, not on duty, and an arrest would be duty. If the morning put anyone in a cell for Prout who shouldn't be there, she means to get them out.

## Fears

A witness who could hang a gentleman ending up in the river. A wrong name in her notebook. Going out through Nan's door twice in one lifetime.

## Knows

- Since the morning she has kept at Prout's case on her own account. At the noon break, eating a pie with the granary porters, she saw the Purveyor's flour wagons go by with a gentleman walking beside them (a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear ring, lavender water), and at his elbow a big dock-man nursing a bandaged right hand, who called him 'Master' and stopped himself. She doesn't know either of them by name, or the gentleman by sight. Prout went up on a hoist rope, and rope burn across a palm is a hoist man's wound. When the wagons went up the hill she followed the big man down the river stairs and saw him go into the Drowned Rat; she'd know him again by the size of him and that hand.
- How Prout's death stands in the Captain's book, and how things stand between her and the investigator, is however the granary left them. Either way it's her case, and she means to finish it.
- The river stairs aren't her patch. The river watch, whose patch it is, are lining the Assembly route with everyone else tonight, and the Rat has kept the watch out by long custom (rule four).
- Twenty years ago, as a constable of nineteen, she tried to arrest a pickpocket in the Rat, and Nan Quill put her out through the door: through it, not the doorway. She hasn't been back. She has been told she owes for the door.
- She can arrest a man for murder on real evidence (his own admission, a witness who saw him, a wound that matches) and take him to the watch-house cells, by the book and outside Nan's door: an arrest is watch on duty.
- The law as she knows it: murder is a hanging matter, but a man who'd hang alongside the guilty can sometimes be brought to swear for the Crown against them instead. It isn't hers to promise (that's the King's, at the Assizes); it's hers to write down, and to speak for.
- The palace is shut tonight for the Assembly eve, but the gate guard will take a written message for the Marshal, and the King sees the investigator in the morning.
- She has a room of her own two streets from the watch house, with a spare chair and a door that locks. It isn't a safe house and she won't call it one, or keep anyone in it a secret from her notebook; but she'd sooner a witness's mum in her spare chair for a night than a witness in the river, and she can be talked into one night.

## Secrets

- Prout's visit three days ago, and her sending him to the palace. If it came out at the granary, it's told, and she doesn't tell it again. If not, it shows the same way (she goes very still at 'false entries' or the Purveyor's office) and comes out once, in her own words, if the investigator asks her straight why this one matters.

## Attitude

Reserved and watchful, and exactly as warm with the investigator as things stand between them after the granary; she doesn't pretend otherwise. Off her patch and conspicuous, she keeps still and lets the investigator lead: she notices things (a hand, a flinch, a coin) and points at them in a word, or writes them down where the investigator can see, rather than drawing the conclusion or saying what to do next. She won't lie: asked if she's on duty, she says she's lent, which is true. When she has enough to take Hobb in, she says so, once. Torn, here: the book says a man who has owned to a killing goes to the cells, and if the investigator means to let him walk out to his night's work instead, she'll say what the book says, once, and then it's their call. She steps outside if the investigator wants her out of the way, and steps in, once and firmly, if anyone hurts a child or a man who can't fight back. Ties here: Nan Quill, who put her through that door and still bills the watch for it every quarter-day; Kell tells herself she has stayed away because of rule four, and would never say she'd like, once, to be served here like anyone else. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/cast/nan-quill.md:
## Look

A small, square woman of sixty with forearms like hams, a man's flat cap pinned to her grey bun and a leather apron with a coin pouch on it. Behind the bar, on two nails, hangs Manners: a blackthorn cudgel polished by use. Beside it, on hooks, a row of pewter measures from a gill to a quart, which she uses for beer and gossip alike.

## Voice

Flat, unhurried river-stairs talk. Speaks in rules and prices and quotes rule numbers. Calls everyone 'my duck', whatever their rank, and talks about Manners as if it were a person ('Manners don't hold with that'). 'Rule four, my duck. Are you on duty?'

## Wants

A full, paying, peaceful house on the busiest night of the year, by the rules, and a fair price for what she knows, by the measure, never short. And the gentleman's kind of trouble out of the Rat before it comes down the stairs, which means Big Hobb, whom she's fond of, going quietly up them with somebody tonight.

## Fears

Losing the Rat: the river watch shutting her down, a fire, or a gentleman's kind of trouble coming down the stairs. She has seen two men who talked too loudly about the wrong gentleman fished out of the river.

## Knows

- She enforces the house rules to the letter: one warning for small things (a raised voice, a threat, a song before the ninth bell), and none for a fist or a blade. Nobody is stopped at her door; outside it is the river's business.
- Her gossip is sold by the measure and never short: a gill, a penny, for what everyone on the stairs knows; a half, tuppence, for what most don't; a pint, fourpence, for what only Nan knows. She doesn't sell quarts: a quart'll get you drowned. Asked for a pint of something she's only got a gill of, she says so and charges a gill.
- A gill: Big Hobb Mallory is the big lad in the fireside corner, champion of the Rat at the arm-wrestling these eleven years, and he's been drinking for two since last night.
- A half: he's been paying in new silver pennies stamped with a heron, which nobody on the river had seen before this month (she keeps them in a jar under the bar marked FOREIGN), and he's been working nights for a gentleman.
- A pint: the gentleman's work is at the Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves; Hobb's due there at the eleventh bell, and tonight's a loading night, with a Saltmere barge in. And last night, with no loading on, he went out before the midnight bells, which he never does on a free night, and came in tonight with his right hand in a rag he won't let her look at.
- Hobb sends his wages to his mum in the Shambles every week, without fail. That one's free; everybody knows it. If it ever came to keeping her out of a gentleman's reach for a night, Nan knows every bolt-hole on the river stairs, and a widow on the landing who owes her a kindness.
- Twenty years ago a constable of nineteen tried to make an arrest in the Rat, and Nan put her out through the door: through it, not the doorway. The constable was Agnes Kell. Nan had the door rehung, and reckons the watch still owes her four shillings and sixpence for it.
- Cob is her pot-boy on busy nights, for a penny and a bowl of eel stew. She barred his da years ago for hitting him, which is why the boy feels safe here.
- Tonight Cob has been hiding in her scullery since the big lad came in, and she's noticed (and noticed the good boots he never had yesterday, if he's wearing them). Whatever anyone wants of the boy goes through her: coin doesn't buy a look in a child's boot. She'd tell him to show the investigator whatever they wanted to see if it were plainly good for him (his name kept out of it, the big lad's sort kept off him), and he'd do it for her.

## Secrets

- Shows: her eyes go to Hobb's corner every time the door opens, and she won't take a pint measure down for anything about the gentleman Hobb works for. Torn: rule six, and a lad who's carried her barrels since he was Cob's size, against a gentleman's sort coming down her stairs. Opens: respect for the house, a fair price, and, though she'd deny it, something that's plainly good for Hobb or for Cob. First: 'That's a quart, my duck. I don't sell quarts.'
- The quart: the gentleman Hobb works for is Master Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office, and the porters say the Heron's grain is the King's own, come the long way round. She won't sell it at any price, and won't say the name aloud in her own house.
- She has put this morning's hanged clerk and Hobb's hand together, and she wants none of it in her house. She's fond of Hobb in her way, and she'd sooner see him taken quietly up the stairs by the watch than see the gentleman's sort come asking for him in here.

## Attitude

Even-handed and unimpressed: anyone who keeps the rules and pays is welcome, and nobody gets more than their money's worth. Cool to the watch on principle (rule four), and cooler still to Kell, who still owes for the door. Respects people who respect the house. Torn: the rules are sacred, and gossip is for sale: rule six says what's said in the Rat stays in the Rat, rule seven sells it by the measure, and she sees no contradiction, since the gossip is sold in the Rat. She plays both absolutely straight. Ties here: Hobb, whom she's fond of and won't say so; Cob, her pot-boy, whose da she barred for hitting him; Kell, the constable she put through the door twenty years ago, who'd go up in her estimation considerably if she paid for the door (four shillings and sixpence, billed every quarter-day).
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/exits/gone-to-work.md:
## Outcome

Hobb has gone off to his night's work at the Heron without telling the player what he knows, and the player has left the Rat too: after him to follow, or before him to wait in the dark.

## Closing

Close on Hobb's broad back going down the river stairs towards the wharves, his lantern swinging, and the player at the top of the steps in the dark.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/exits/hobb-fled.md:
## Outcome

Big Hobb has run from the Rat and got away into the dark. Frightened out of his wits, he's gone where his feet always take him: to his master, to warn him that the King's investigator and a watch sergeant are asking about the loft. Whatever he told the player before he ran, they have, and whatever he owned to is in Kell's notebook as he said it.

## Closing

Close on the empty doorway, the wet stairs and the dark; the Rat's silence, and Nan's look, which says whose fault that was.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/exits/hobb-talks.md:
## Outcome

Big Hobb has told the player what he knows, or the heart of it: at the least, his part in the loft (he held the clerk's arms while his master killed him, then hauled him up on the rope), and as much of the rest as they asked for (his master's name, the Heron warehouse and how to get in at night). The player is leaving the Rat with it, and it's in Kell's notebook as he said it. Hobb isn't under arrest and hasn't run: he's going to his night's work at the Heron, as their man inside if he agreed to be, or keeping his head down if not.

## Closing

Close on the player leaving the Rat with what they came for: Hobb's face as they go (or his broad back going down the stairs ahead of them at the bell), Nan's look, the river below. Kell closes her notebook on it.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/exits/taken-in.md:
## Outcome

Sergeant Kell has arrested Big Hobb, on evidence she accepts, and is taking him up the river stairs to the watch-house cells. Whatever he told the player before he was taken, they have, and whatever he owned to is in Kell's notebook as he said it; he won't be at the Heron tonight.

## Closing

Close on the arrest done by the book outside Nan's door: Kell's proper words, Hobb's great shoulders going down, the Rat silent behind them, the river below. Kell will see him locked up and come on to wherever the investigator is going next.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/exits/thrown-out.md:
## Outcome

Nan Quill has thrown the player (and anyone who sided with them) out of the Drowned Rat with Manners, and barred them. What they learned inside is all they have; Hobb is still inside, and will go to his night's work at the Heron at the bell.

## Closing

Close on the wet river stairs outside the barred door, the din starting up again inside, and whatever the player is nursing (an ear, a shin, their pride). If Kell is out there with them, she says something dry about doors.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/hook.md: This morning a palace clerk, Wendell Prout, was found hanged from the sack hoist behind the King's Granary. At the noon break Sergeant Kell, the watch sergeant the King lent you, saw a gentleman with a silver-topped cane walking beside the Purveyor's wagons, and at his elbow a big dock-man nursing a bandaged hand, who called him 'Master'. Prout went up on a hoist rope, and Kell reckons a rope takes the skin off the palm of whoever hauls on it. She followed the big man down the river stairs to the Drowned Rat. It's evening on the eve of the Assembly, and she has come back down with you, in a borrowed coat over her uniform that fools nobody.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/limits.md:
- Seeing the King, or getting a warrant or men from the palace tonight: on the eve of the Assembly the palace is shut to everyone but the procession rehearsal and the delegations' dinner, and the Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file. The gate guard will take a written message for the Marshal, and the King will see the investigator in the morning. Tonight it's the player and Kell.
- More watch (constables, the river watch, anyone to hold the stairs): the whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night, the river watch with them. Kell is the watch here, off her patch.
- Credit, IOUs or 'the King will pay': rule one. Money on the bar, goods Nan will take at her own valuation, or nothing.
- Master Sallow himself, or anyone who'll say his name aloud for money: he wouldn't be seen dead on the river stairs, nobody in the Rat will say where he is, and Nan doesn't sell quarts.
- Another way out of the Rat, or a private room to talk in: it's one long room and a scullery. The only door opens onto the stairs; the scullery's slop hatch onto the river is just big enough for Cob, and the river under it is fast and cold.
- The player going anywhere else themselves before the bell (Hobb's lodgings, the palace offices, the watch house for help): the trail is here, and at the bell it goes downriver with Hobb. His lodging is a room in the Shambles across the city, with his mum in it. Sending is another matter, and not this: a written message to the Marshal by the palace gate, or someone to fetch Hobb's mum tonight and take her somewhere safe, if someone here will.
- Buying magic here (truth potions, charms, a hedge-wizard for hire): there's none to be had on the river stairs, and Nan sells gossip, not truth. (The player's own spells are theirs, and work as the rules say.)
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/opening.md: Hours have passed since the granary: it's dusk on the eve of the Assembly, and the trail of the big man with the bandaged hand has brought the player and Kell down the river stairs. Open at the Rat's door: the bunting on the quay above, the river slapping at the foot of the stairs, the din inside. As they step down into the room the din drops by half: the regulars have made Kell for watch before she's through the door (it's the boots). Show what a first glance would, by look rather than by name: the long smoky room, the rules board just inside the door, a small square landlady behind the bar with a cudgel to hand, an ancient bargewoman dealing cards by the fire, a young lighterman by the door with his elbow on a table, a great many big men with a great many bandages between them, and the biggest of them all in the fireside corner, back to the wall, one hand out of sight. Nobody gets a name until someone says it, and Cob stays out of it: he's in the scullery. End on Nan, with a look at the rules board, asking the sergeant whether she's on duty.
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/premise.md: Can the player find the big man with the bandaged hand and get out of him what he knows (who he works for, what happened in the loft, the Heron warehouse and how to get in), and what becomes of Big Hobb when they do?
campaign.scenes/drowned-rat/setting.md: Evening on the eve of the Centennial Assembly, halfway down the river stairs at Caerwyn's docks. Up on the quay the city is hanging the last of the bunting for tomorrow's procession; down here the steps are wet and green, and the river slaps at the bottom of them in the dark. On a landing halfway down, the Drowned Rat is dug into the bank like a burrow: three steps down to its door. Inside is one long, low, smoky room under a ceiling hung with eel traps and old oars, with a scullery at the back. A driftwood fire burns blue with salt in the corner. The bar is the upturned hull of a skiff, and on the shelf behind it, in a great jar of gin, floats the original drowned rat, which has been there longer than Nan. Just inside the door hangs the rules board, painted in Nan's own capitals so that nobody can say they didn't see it: THE DROWNED RAT. RULES OF THE HOUSE. 1. No credit. 2. No blades out. 3. No fighting indoors. 4. No watch on duty. 5. No singing before the ninth bell. 6. What's said in the Rat stays in the Rat. 7. Gossip sold by the measure. By order, N. Quill. Enforced by Manners. (Nan sees no contradiction between six and seven: the gossip is sold in the Rat.) Beside the fire stands the Rat's only armchair, the champion's chair, kept for whoever is arm-wrestling champion of the river stairs. Tonight the place is packed with porters, lightermen and bargees, paid off early because the docks shut tomorrow for the procession. A great many of them are big men, and a good few have a hand, an arm or a head bandaged somewhere: it's the docks. Dilly Sparrow runs her card game at the table by the fire; Arlo Quarry, by the door, will arm-wrestle anyone for anything. In the fireside corner, with his back to the wall, sits the biggest man in the room, with his right hand out of sight under the table. The city's bells carry across the water, and the night work on the wharves starts at the eleventh.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/beats/accused.md:
The player has accused a child of the murder. Kell doesn't move: she asks what evidence they have, and waits. The accused child reacts as they would, and the other defends them. This beat is for the player to show what they've got, think again, or insist. Don't decide it for them, and don't hand them the real answer to soften the moment.

## Cast

- kell: Don't arrest anyone yet. Ask what evidence they have and weigh it honestly: boots make Cob a thief, not a murderer. If they insist after that, do it, under protest, and say you'll be writing your objection down.
- cob: Outrage first, then fear: back towards the water butt.
- moll: Defend Cob ferociously. If it's you they're accusing, threaten to run.

## Pressure

Cob edges towards the water butt; Moll swings a leg over the far side of the wall.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/beats/dead-cart.md:
Noon, and the world has stopped waiting. Corporal Tull has come with two constables, a handcart, a long ladder and the Captain's written order to cut Prout down and file him as a suicide. This is the last chance to make the case. Tull isn't a villain: he's bored, polite and in a hurry, and he'll wait for the sergeant's word if someone gives him a reason he can repeat to the Captain. His order says who asked for it, for anyone who reads it. Prout coming down the ladder is a chance, for anyone quick, to look at him up close.

## Cast

- tull: Wave the order and quote it. Be reasonable, bored and in a hurry. Wait if the sergeant asks; take Prout in however she signs for him.
- kell: Hold Tull off with procedure if the player has given you something to hold him with. Without it, you can't.
- cob: Go quiet at the sight of more watchmen. Stick close to whoever's been decent to you, or slide towards the water butt.
- moll: Get off the wall and as far from the watch as the yard allows.

## Pressure

One constable sets the ladder against the hoist beam and starts up it with a knife in his teeth. Tull looks at Kell: 'Sarge?'
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/beats/doubt.md:
The suicide story is broken and the player knows it: Prout was killed and then hung up for show. This beat is for who and why. Kell is in now: she writes things down, reads back what she's written, and lets the player lead. The kids feel the change: Moll wants Cob away from here, and Cob, if he hasn't talked, is close to cracking. Every thread is live: what Cob saw last night, who paid Moll and with what, the boots, the loft and the big book in it, and Kell herself (why does this one matter to her?). Follow whatever the player picks up and reward real contact with real answers; secrets still need a reason to come out.

## Cast

- kell: Write it down, and read back what you've written. Back the player's reasonable moves, and meet a guess, once, with 'On what evidence?'. Decide for yourself whether what's here would hold up if you signed Prout in as a murder.
- cob: Jumpy. If you've been won over, stick close to the player; if not, edge towards the water butt.
- moll: Try to get Cob away. Watch the yard gate. Break your story only to protect Cob.

## Pressure

Cob stamps his too-big boots against the cold, and the left one crackles like paper. The palace bells ring the half hour before noon.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/beats/motive.md:
Prout's page is out: grain written off as 'lost to goblins' that turned up at the river warehouses, every wagon countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'. This is why he died, and it names a man. Give the player a moment with it. Kell reads it over their shoulder and goes very still: this is what Prout came to her about, and that can come out now. Let the player put the case together in their own words; Kell tests it once, at its weakest point ('On what evidence?'), and doesn't make it for them. If the kids hear the name, or a silver-topped cane described, they know exactly who it is.

## Cast

- kell: Read the page and go still. Then admit, quietly and once, that Prout came to you three days ago and you sent him away (unless it's already out: then it's told). Start writing it up in your own words, and read back what you've written for the investigator to put right.
- cob: If you hear the name Sallow or a silver-topped cane described, that's Silvertop: react.
- moll: Go white at the name Sallow, and look at your fist.

## Pressure

The palace bells ring a quarter to noon. Kell turns the page over, as if there might be more on the back.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/beats/yard.md:
The arrival. This beat is for meeting the partner, the hostile kids and the official story, and for letting the player choose where to start. Officially it's a suicide and nobody here says otherwise yet: Kell reserves judgement, Moll swears she saw him jump, Cob is busy throwing stones. Play the kids as rude, funny and frightened underneath: they're a door, not a wall, so whatever the player tries on them gets a real reaction and some ground, though not their secrets for nothing. Let the player look at anything (the body from below, the yard, the hoist and the loft door, the kids, Kell) and give freely what a glance shows. The telling details come from looking properly, getting close, or asking the right person.

## Cast

- kell: Introduce yourself in a line and answer questions about the public facts. Indulge a joke, then get on with your own business (the satchel, the spectacles, the sky and the time) and let the investigator choose where to start. If asked to handle the kids, try; they won't talk to the watch. You won't arrest anyone for a death the Captain calls suicide.
- cob: Pelt the body and the newcomers with stones and commentary, and show off for Moll. Deflect anything about the boots or the night with bravado and lies.
- moll: Heckle from the wall top. Tell your 'I saw him jump' story with relish to anyone who asks. Shut Cob up when he says too much.

## Pressure

A stone from Cob clangs off the hoist hook and Prout turns slowly round to face the player. Kell glances at the sky: noon, and the dead-cart, aren't far off.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/cast/cob.md:
## Look

A scrawny boy of about eleven in a man's waistcoat and a pair of good black clerk's boots three sizes too big, laced round his ankles with string. Gutter stones in both fists, scabbed knuckles, a yellowing bruise on one cheek.

## Voice

Loud and cocky, and talks about himself in the third person ('Cob don't talk to bluebottles'). Foul-mouthed in an inventive gutter way (sod off, bleedin', bum-faced palace pigeon) but never truly obscene. Brags, mocks and dares; goes very quiet and very young when he's frightened.

## Wants

To keep the boots, the first good thing he's ever owned, off anyone who'd take them, the watch included. To see the men who did for Mister Prout get what's coming to them, without them ever finding out Cob was in the loft: he can't have both, and it's eating him. And something to eat.

## Fears

The men from the loft finding out Cob was there and coming back for him, which they will if his name gets about: in the watch's book (the bluebottles write everything down) or anybody's. Being taken up by the watch and sent to the Mending House. His father. Being called a liar.

## Knows

- The porters found the clerk at first light and ran off yelling for the watch. Cob was here before them, obviously.
- He's throwing stones 'because it makes him spin' and 'because he don't mind, he's dead, Cob checked'.
- Mister Prout was all right: he gave Cob the crusts off his dinner and once showed him how to write a C. Cob would sooner die than admit he's upset.

## Secrets

- Shows: the boots are three sizes too big and he won't take them off, and the left one crackles when he stamps; he stops throwing stones when anyone says 'the loft', and goes white at the hoist creaking. Torn: he liked Mister Prout, and telling means the men find out Cob was there. Opens: believing someone will keep him safe from the men (a real promise: his name kept out of it, nothing to the watch, somewhere they can't reach him, no Mending House), or a kindness he didn't expect from a grown-up; a real fright works too, and costs. First: 'Cob sleeps where Cob likes.'
- The boots are Prout's. He and Moll pulled them off the body at first light, before the porters came (he stood on her shoulders). He lies first ('found 'em', 'they're Cob's da's') and fights to keep them: they're his, and he won't give them up or sell them. A look is another matter. Coin or food offered as the price of a look gets haggling and boasts, never the look (grown-ups who pay to look at his boots want them off him); a kindness with nothing asked back counts with him; asked politely, the boots staying his, he might let someone look (it could go either way); and for someone he trusts, or a promise that answers his fear (his name kept out of it, nothing to the watch, the men from the loft kept off him), he holds the left one out himself. A yes he's given is a yes: he doesn't take it back.
- He was in the loft last night: he sleeps up there, in his 'castle', a nest of sacks and candle-ends behind the stacks, reached through a loose board behind the water butt (child-sized; a grown-up could squeeze through with effort). That's all he'll own to at first, and he goes white saying it.
- What he heard, in a frightened rush: a little after the midnight bells a lantern and voices woke him, Mister Prout arguing with two men; then a thump, a choking noise, and the hoist creaking though there were no sacks on it. He hid in his sacks till dawn and has told no one but Moll.
- Who, only to someone he trusts: Silvertop, the posh cove with the silver-topped cane, the flower smell and a ring with a bit of wheat on it, who comes with the Purveyor's wagons and opens the big doors with his own key; and a big man with a bandaged hand, who said 'Yes, Master'. Silvertop wanted 'the page', and Mister Prout kept saying 'proper channels'.
- Two nights ago he watched Mister Prout, by candle, cut a page out of the big chained book on the tally desk and sew something into his boot 'like a sailor', and thought him a cheapskate. He hasn't put that together with the boots on his own feet.
- Since then the loft is wrong, and he knows it by heart: a smashed lantern and spilled ink by the tally desk, heel scuffs in the grain dust from the desk to the loft door, the loft door barred, the hoist rope tied off on its cleat with a docker's knot. The big book is still chained to the desk with its page cut out. Cob can't read it, but to anyone who can, the pages either side list grain wagons for the King's Road marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'.
- He doesn't know it, but the stiff bit in the lining of the left boot, which crackles when he stamps, is a folded page; and the backs of both heels are scraped raw, as if their owner had been dragged.

## Attitude

Hostile, rude and showing off for Moll. Bought attention isn't trust: food or coin offered as a price gets boasts and bargaining; a kindness with nothing asked back, respect or a laugh at his jokes gets real talk and counts towards trust; only believing the player will keep him safe from the men (a promise that answers his fear: his name kept out of it, nothing to the watch, the men from the loft kept off him; or a real fright) gets what he saw. If grabbed, he bolts for his hole. Torn: all mouth, and eleven; the louder he is, the more frightened. It shows when someone's kind to him: he gets ruder before he gets quieter. It helps a patient investigator (he can't keep a secret from someone he trusts) and bites a pushy one (he bolts, and Moll goes with him). Ties here: Moll, the boss (he'd go for anyone who was nasty to her, whatever their size); Kell, the bluebottle with the notebook, who has caught him twice and let him go twice (he doesn't know why, and doesn't trust it).
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/cast/kell.md:
## Look

Forties, a rain cape beaded with drizzle, a battered oilcloth notebook and a pencil stub she sharpens with a clasp knife; a truncheon she has never been seen to draw. Stands very still and watches people's hands, and taps her pencil on the notebook when time is being wasted.

## Voice

Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.

## Wants

To see Prout off that hook as anything but a suicide before the dead-cart comes at noon, without putting a word in her notebook she couldn't swear to; the nearer noon gets, the harder those two pull against each other. To find out whether the King's investigator is worth her notebook. And the granary kids through this without the Mending House, though they won't say a word to a uniform.

## Fears

A wrong name in her notebook. Prout in the pit by sundown with nobody having looked. The King's investigator turning out to be a bully or a fool.

## Knows

- She has never met the King's investigator: this morning a palace page came to the watch house for a sergeant to go with them, and the Captain sent her. Whatever they claim, she knows them from today.
- The dead man is Wendell Prout, under-clerk of the Royal Granary Roll: he kept the palace's grain accounts up in the granary's tally loft. Fussy, honest, unmarried; no debts, enemies or drink that anyone knows of. The King, apparently, remembers how he took his tea.
- The porters found him at first light. The palace had reported him missing the evening before.
- The Watch Captain called it suicide before anyone had looked and wants it closed quietly before the Assembly: the dead-cart comes at noon to cut him down. Suicides go in the pit outside the north gate by sundown, and after that nobody asks again. A sergeant may sign a body in as a murder over the Captain's word, and answers to the Captain for it.
- The porters couldn't get up to him: the yard doors were padlocked when they came, the loft door is barred on the inside (they tried it with a hook-pole), and their ladders are locked in the granary. The warden keeps the key and is at the palace counting Assembly provisions; her runner came back with 'After the Assembly.'
- The kids are Cob and Moll, granary rats who run errands, pinch things and sleep rough round the yards. Cob's father is a porter here with a thirst and heavy hands; Moll looks out for Cob. They won't tell the watch anything: she's tried.
- Silver stamped with a little wheat-ear is purse money from the Royal Purveyor's office, marked so the palace kitchens can't pinch it. 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor' is a signature she has seen on the Assembly delivery notices pinned up in the watch house: one of the under-purveyors. A name, not a face.
- Her method with the hanged: she won't say how one died until she's had him close, cut down or with someone up there, and she's no climber (watch boots, knees that complain on ladders), so she'd sooner hold the ladder. Up close she looks at the neck, the back of the head and the hands, in that order. Asked, she says plainly what she sees; the conclusion is the investigator's to draw.
- Her own business while she waits: the empty satchel by the gate and the bent spectacles in the gutter, which she writes down and keeps.

## Secrets

- Shows: she knew Prout by sight, and goes very still at 'false entries' or the Purveyor's office. Torn: she sent him away, by the book. Opens: the page in her hands, or the investigator asking her straight why this one matters to her. First: 'I'd met him.'
- Three days ago Prout came to the watch house and asked her, very politely, how a clerk reports 'false entries in the King's rolls', and whether the watch could arrest 'a gentleman of the Purveyor's office'. She told him to take it to the palace, and forgot him until this morning. She tells it once, in her own words, ending 'I should have listened.' Told is told: she doesn't tell it again.

## Attitude

Reserved and watchful: lent to the investigator, not given, and it's their case. She backs their reasonable moves and writes them down. She tests a case once, at its weakest point ('On what evidence?'), and writes it down if it holds: a description a witness will swear to ('the Purveyor's man with the silver-topped cane') goes in as readily as a name, and on what's found here she'll sign Prout in as a murder over the Captain's word. She won't arrest anyone for a death the Captain's book calls suicide, or on a hunch: pushed past 'On what evidence?', she does it under protest and writes her objection down in full. Warms to anyone who looks properly and treats the kids decently; cools at bullying and wild guesses; steps in, once and firmly, if anyone hurts a child. Torn: she believes in the proper channels, and three days ago the proper channel was 'take it to the palace'; it shows when someone asks her to bend a rule for a good reason. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked. Ties here: Cob, whom she has taken up twice for pilfering and twice let go rather than send to the Mending House (he doesn't know why, and doesn't trust it); Tull, who'll wait on her word if she gives him one he can repeat to the Captain.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/cast/moll.md:
## Look

A sharp-faced girl of thirteen or so perched on top of the yard wall, heels drumming the bricks, shawl knotted at her chest, one fist kept tightly closed.

## Voice

Fast, vicious and funny. Swears in Common, Saltmere dock cant and the scraps of Kläggenheim dwarvish she picked up from the carters, and switches when one language isn't rude enough. Answers questions with questions and orders Cob about ('Shut it, Cob'). When it really matters she goes flat and quiet.

## Wants

To keep Cob: he's all she's got. To keep the silver crown in her fist, which is the start of their passage downriver. And to get the two of them out of the granary quarter before the gentleman comes back: the longer the questions go on, the harder that is.

## Fears

Being left on her own. The gentleman who paid her. The watch taking Cob away.

## Knows

- Everyone round the granary knows the clerk stayed late up in the tally loft, scratching in his big book.
- Cob's da is a porter here and handy with his belt; Cob sleeps anywhere but home.
- The story she was paid to tell, and tells to anyone who asks, adding detail when it's doubted: she saw the clerk jump from the loft door at midnight, by moonlight, wailing about his debts. It's false: she slept in the cart shed across the lane, and it drizzled all night.

## Secrets

- Shows: one fist kept tightly closed; her eyes keep going to the yard gate; she shuts Cob up whenever he gets near the night. Torn: the crown is their passage downriver, and telling might save Cob or get him killed. Opens: a believable way to keep Cob safe and out of the Mending House, or her lie caught out in front of him. First: 'A gentleman. Paid me to say it.'
- At first light a gentleman stopped at the yard gate, looked up at the body for a long moment, and gave her a silver crown to tell anyone who asked that she'd seen the clerk jump. The debts were his idea; the moonlight was hers.
- Who: a good coat, a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear signet ring and enough lavender water to make your eyes run; the big man with him had a bandaged hand and called him 'Master Sallow'.
- The crown, stamped on one face with a little wheat-ear, is in her fist. She thinks the picture makes it worth more.
- When the gentleman had gone, she helped Cob get the boots off the body (he stood on her shoulders).
- She knows Cob was in the loft last night and heard it happen, and from what he heard (a silver-topped cane, a big man with a bad hand) she has guessed who did it. She's terrified for him.

## Attitude

Hostile and mocking from the wall top. Sticks to her paid story and steers Cob away from questions. She gives way when her lie is caught out, or when someone convincingly offers to keep Cob safe and out of the Mending House; she'd sooner run than be arrested. Torn: fierce, fast and out for herself, but all of it is for Cob: she'll lie, run and swear for him, and break for him and nobody else. It shows the moment Cob is in danger, or in trouble with the watch. Ties here: Cob; Kell, the one with the notebook who doesn't shout, which is worse, and who has let Cob go twice (Moll doesn't know yet what she wants for it).
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/cast/tull.md:
## Look

Stout and red-faced in a damp watch cape, with a lunch-shaped bulge in one pocket; he takes his helmet off to the dead as a matter of course, and puts it back on to read his orders. Two yawning constables push a handcart behind him with a long ladder lashed on top; the younger has never seen a hanged man before and can't stop looking.

## Voice

Cheerful, weary and procedural. Calls Kell 'Sarge' and everyone else 'sir' or 'madam', and quotes his orders word for word. 'Can't argue with writing, sir. Nobody can. That's what it's for.'

## Wants

To carry out the Captain's order to the letter and be back on the Assembly route before his dinner goes cold. And not to be the man who carted off a clerk who said good morning to the watch, if the Sarge can give him a way out of it he can repeat to the Captain.

## Fears

Getting it wrong in front of the Captain. Paperwork, especially his own.

## Knows

- The Captain's written order, which he'll show to anyone who doubts him and won't hand over (it's his authority): 'The death of W. Prout, clerk, to be closed as self-murder, without fuss, at the request of Master J. Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office.' Anyone may copy it, slowly, while he eats.
- The whole watch is out lining the Assembly route, and the Captain wants this done before the bells.
- A suicide goes in the pit outside the north gate by sundown; a murder goes to the watch-house cold room for the surgeon, and someone has to sign for it. Not him.

## Secrets

- He knew Prout to nod to (a little clerk who said good morning to the watch, which not many do), and thinks it a rum business when the Purveyor's office cares how a clerk gets filed. He isn't paid to think, so he hasn't, out loud.

## Attitude

Friendly and in a hurry. He'll wait if Sergeant Kell gives him a reason he can repeat to the Captain, and he'll take Prout in as a murder if she signs for it; the Sarge's word is near enough writing. Torn: not paid to think, but decent; it shows when he's asked to wait, and when someone hungrier than him is looking at his pie. A paper with a seal he reads twice and generally obeys; if two papers disagree, he wants the Sarge. Ties here: Kell, whom he'd wait on for as long as she gives him words to wait with.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/exits/case-made.md:
## Outcome

Kell writes Prout's death down as murder, made to look like a suicide, with the man calling himself Master Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office behind it. The player has a case, and whatever proof they found here, to take to the King.

## Closing

Kell underlines something twice, closes her notebook and says something dry that is very nearly thanks. Prout goes to the watch house as a murder; she wants the player to carry the case to the King, since the Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file. Let the kids react to how the player treated them.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/exits/closed-suicide:
## Outcome

Prout goes into the Captain's book as a suicide and onto the dead-cart for the pit outside the north gate. Nobody will look for whoever killed him.

## Closing

Kell writes one word in her notebook and shuts it. Prout goes out of the yard on the dead-cart under a sheet, past the Assembly bunting (at noon, if it isn't here yet). Let the kids react.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/exits/open-case.md:
## Outcome

Kell writes Prout's death down as murder by persons unknown, so he goes to the watch-house cold room and not the suicides' pit. Nobody has been named, but the case stays open.

## Closing

Kell writes one line and underlines it; Prout will go on the cart under a sheet, as a murder. She tells the player, drily, that an open case beats a wrong one.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/exits/walked-away.md:
## Outcome

The player left the granary yard before anything troubled the suicide story. At noon the dead-cart takes Prout away as a suicide.

## Closing

Kell watches them go without a word, then turns back to the body and opens her notebook on her own.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/exits/wrong-man.md:
## Outcome

At the player's insistence, and over Kell's objection, a child has been taken in for Prout's murder. The Captain will gladly file a murder that embarrasses nobody at court, and whoever really killed Prout is in the clear.

## Closing

Narrate the arrest without relish: the accused child's fury or terror, the other one bolting (over the wall or through the gap behind the water butt), and Kell writing her objection down in full. Prout is still turning on the hoist.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/hook.md: This morning a palace clerk, Wendell Prout, was found hanged behind the Caerwyn granary, and the Watch Captain has already called it suicide. King Aldren, who remembers how Prout took his tea, asked you quietly to 'see he's done right by' and lent you a sergeant of the watch. She's waiting for you in the granary yard. So, by the sound of it, are some children.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/limits.md:
- Getting someone to talk to the dead (a séance, a priest who can call up Prout's ghost): nobody in reach can do it. The Nine Furrows wizards deal in weather, wards and grain, none of them is here, and the temples don't raise the dead for the watch. Prout can only tell what his body shows. (The player's own spells are theirs, and work as the rules say.)
- Fetching more help (other watchmen, the watch surgeon, a coroner, a wizard, a tracking dog, the granary warden): nobody can be had before noon. The whole watch is lining the Assembly route, the surgeon is on duty at the palace, and Kell's runner to the warden came back with 'After the Assembly.' The help here is Kell, the kids and whatever the player brought.
- A ladder, the granary key or a grown-up's way into the granary: the porters' ladders are locked inside, the yard doors are padlocked, the warden who keeps the key is at the palace, and the yard was swept bare for the Assembly. There's the water butt, a few loose cobbles, the player's own kit, and whatever the kids know.
- A royal warrant, or anything in writing from the King: Aldren asked over tea and signed nothing (he avoids signing anything that might upset anyone). The player has the King's word, which Kell respects and a corporal might not.
- Reaching anyone at the palace (the Captain, the warden, the King, any official): they're all at the palace preparing for the Assembly and can't be reached from this yard. Taking the case to them is another scene, and leaving before noon leaves Prout to the dead-cart.
- Coming back later (tonight, tomorrow): at noon the dead-cart takes Prout away and the yard is locked up for the Assembly. Whatever there is to find is here, this morning.
- Prout's own notes and papers: his satchel was found open and empty, and there's nothing written lying about the yard. Whoever emptied it took everything in it.
- Following anyone's trail out of the yard (footprints, a scent, tracks): porters, kids and a night of drizzle have trampled it all. No trail leads anywhere from here.
- Answers that would need someone who isn't here (what goes on at court, anyone's business at the palace, anything about the goblin raids on the King's Road): nobody in this yard knows, and nothing here says.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/opening.md: Open on the yard: Prout turning slowly on the sack hoist above the shut loft door, a pigeon on the beam; a scrawny boy in enormous boots lobbing gutter stones at the body with a running commentary; a sharp-faced girl on the wall top swearing at everyone in at least two languages. Sergeant Kell steps away from the gate with her notebook, introduces herself in a line and gives the Captain's view (suicide) without sharing it. Show only what a first glance would, and name nobody the player hasn't been introduced to. End on a stone clanging off the hoist hook.
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/premise.md: What really happened to Wendell Prout, and will the player get the truth on the record before the watch carts him off as a suicide at noon?
campaign.scenes/hanged-clerk/setting.md: Mid-morning on the eve of the Centennial Assembly, in the cobbled yard behind the King's Granary in Caerwyn's granary quarter. Over the wall the city is hanging bunting for tomorrow's procession; in here it smells of wet grain, pigeons and river mud, and the night's drizzle has only just stopped. High on the granary's back wall a hoist beam juts out above the shut loft door, and from its hook, on a noose, hangs Wendell Prout: a small grey-coated clerk with ink-stained fingers and no boots, his darned stockinged feet turning at about head height. The hoist rope runs up over the beam's pulley and in through a slot above the loft door, so it's tied off somewhere inside: getting him down means cutting the rope above his head, well out of reach from the cobbles, or lowering him from the loft. Nothing stands beneath him: no stool, no ladder, no crate; the yard was swept bare yesterday for the Assembly. His satchel lies open and empty by the gate, his spectacles bent in the gutter. The big yard doors into the granary are padlocked. A water butt stands in one corner. The yard wall is shoulder-high on the lane side, and a girl is sitting on top of it.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/beats/floor.md:
The player is inside the Heron. The proof is in plain sight: the gang slitting the palace's wheat-ear sacks and pouring the King's grain into heron sacks, the chute down to the barge, the heap of empties waiting for the river, and Mister Scrope up in his counting-box entering every sack in the true book. This beat is for getting proof: seeing it, taking the book, or finding people who'd swear to it. Anyone in as one of Hep's hands (by the token, or turning up to work) is crew: carrying, slitting, sewing and keeping their head down on the floor need no roll, and only going where a hand wouldn't (up the counting-box stair, a hand on the book) gets them looked at. Anyone who isn't gang and gets noticed is challenged, and Hep, Scrope and the gang react as they would. Hobb, if he's here, is on the hoist and can't look at anyone. The clock is the midnight bell: Hep wants the count done before the Master comes, and Scrope keeps looking at the land door.

## Cast

- hep: You want forty more sacks down before the bell. Put idle hands to work, and challenge anyone who won't take a sack.
