- scrope: Count, enter, blot, apologise. Keep your hand on the book.
- hobb: If you're here, work the hoist one-handed and don't look at the player.
- kell: If you're inside, watch and remember. If you're on the wharf, keep it.
- saul: Keep the land door, and get up at the bell.

## Pressure

Hep bellows the count: forty to go before the Master. Scrope wipes his pen and looks at the land door. One of the gang, a sack on his shoulder, stops and looks at the player for a long moment.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/beats/midnight.md:
Master Sallow is here, a minute behind his lavender, with his lantern-boy and the Crakes: in at the land door to see the last sacks down, take his share and initial tonight's page in the true book. Everything on the floor changes: the gang work faster and quieter, Scrope stands, Saul holds the door, Duchess growls, and Hobb (if he's here) can't look at anyone. If he has been warned, he's sharp and hurried, wants the book aboard the barge, and has the Crakes look along the wharf. If he finds the player held, or finds them at all, he deals with them his way: his office first, then money, then the Crakes and the river. This is the climax: hide and watch him sign, catch him in the act before witnesses who'll swear (Kell, Hep's gang, Scrope, Hobb), take the book from under his nose, bluff him, or be caught by him. The barge goes at the second bell, whoever has said what.

## Cast

- sallow: You want the barge loaded, the page initialled and your share in your purse. Find fault with something, then climb to the counting-box and initial tonight's page at Scrope's desk, in front of whoever is on the floor. If you find intruders: papers, then money, then the Crakes. Keep the book out of their hands. Exposed in front of witnesses you can't buy, with a sergeant saying the words of arrest and your Crakes still at your side, you don't come quietly: the sword comes out of the cane, and you set the Crakes on them.
- kell: This is the investigator's case and their moment: back their play. You can arrest Sallow if you see him take the King's grain, by the book and out loud, and you will when the investigator calls for it or plainly gives you the moment; never over their plan or instead of it. If they mean to slip away with the proof, go with them. If you're on the wharf, come at their signal or the first shout.
- hep: Keep the gang working and your head down, and watch who looks likeliest to keep your gang off the gallows.
- scrope: Present the book to the Master with shaking hands.
- hobb: If you're here, you can't look at the Master, or at the player.
- saul: Hold the land door for the Master, and keep Duchess off his ankles.

## Pressure

If he hasn't yet, Sallow climbs to the counting-box: Scrope presents the book with shaking hands, and Sallow initials tonight's page and counts his heron pennies into his purse, in plain view of the floor (the moment to catch him at it, for anyone who means to). Then he takes out his watch: the ebb won't wait. He orders the last sacks down and the hatches battened, and out on the river the bargees start singling up their lines.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/beats/wharf.md:
The player is outside the Heron on the dark wharf, and nobody inside knows they're here. This beat is for looking and choosing how to go in. Answer questions about the outside concretely and generously: the land door with Saul, his brazier and Duchess; the plank walk along the piles to the river door and its grille; the barge alongside and the hoist swinging sacks into her; the gang glimpsed through the river door, slitting sacks; the lamp in the counting-box window; the tide on the turn. Kell works out with the player where she's most use. Preparations the player makes should pay off in position and surprise, and a diversion (a noise down the wharf, a barge line slipped, something for Duchess to chase) can draw Saul or the gang away for a moment; a naked flame anywhere near the grain dust is a very bad idea, and everyone at the Heron knows it. Getting in is a real edge, but there are several doors into it, and some need no dice: Hobb's token at the river door, Hobb himself if he's on their side, or a sack on the shoulder and a place in Hep's short-handed gang.

## Cast

- saul: You want a quiet night: mind the land door, talk to Duchess, and get up at the bell to walk the wharf with your lantern.
- kell: Say where you'll be, once: left to choose, out here on the wharf with your whistle, where you can see who comes and goes; at the investigator's elbow if they want a witness inside.
- hep: You want hands and the count: drive the gang, and shout for help at the river door.
- hobb: If you're here, you're on the hoist. If you agreed at the Rat to let them in, you're listening for their knock.

## Pressure

Saul heaves himself up for his round and comes along the wharf with his lantern and Duchess, straight towards wherever the player is standing. Or a sack splits on the hoist and spills grain across the wharf at the player's feet, the wheat-ear stamp plain on the torn sacking.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/cast/hep.md:
## Look

A broad woman in a leather apron with a sack-needle stuck through her collar and a knife on a cord, floured white to the elbows, with a voice like a winch. Her gang work fast, heads down, and don't talk.

## Voice

Shouts in numbers and the gang's own cant ('Forty to the hatch! Mind that seam!'). Never uses a name if 'you' will do. Swears by the tide. 'I don't know whose it is. I know how many there are.'

## Wants

Forty more sacks down to the barge before the Master comes at the midnight bell, so he's nothing to find fault with, and the gang's double pay on the nail. And her gang, her boy Kit first, kept off the gallows, which nothing she's doing tonight will help.

## Fears

The gallows: receiving the King's grain is a hanging matter, and she knows it. The Master. Missing the tide.

## Knows

- Two hundred sacks tonight, forty still to go before the Master comes at the midnight bell to see the last of them down and initial the clerk's count. The barge sails on the ebb at the second bell.
- The palace sacks are slit, poured into heron sacks and sewn shut; the empty wheat-ear sacks go in the river at the end of the night, weighted with stones.
- The gang is short-handed tonight (Assembly eve: half the river's drunk), and she'll put any strong pair of hands to work and ask who they are afterwards.

## Secrets

- Shows: she never says whose grain it is, and turns any question into a count; she looks at her gang, not at the Master, whenever he speaks. Torn: swearing against the Master might save the gang or hang them. Opens: proof the Master will fall (a sergeant arresting him, the true book in someone else's hands, his nerve cracking in front of her gang) and a promise she can believe that those who swear for the Crown won't hang. First: 'Gentlemen don't hang. Porters do.'
- She knows exactly whose grain it is, and that receiving it is a hanging matter, and has never once said so out loud.
- She skims a sack a night for the gang's families: a notch a night on the tally stick in her apron pocket, in nobody's book but hers.
- Her gang comes before everything. To keep them off the gallows she'd swear against the Master in a heartbeat, if she believed it would work, and the gang would stand behind her.

## Attitude

Brusque, practical and suspicious of anyone not working: anyone with a sack on their shoulder is crew until proven otherwise. Cares for her gang like a hen for her chicks, and for nobody else. Torn: a hard woman to everyone but six porters in grain-white; it shows when anyone threatens one of them, or when the King's name is put on them like a shield ('They've got children'). She doesn't fight for the Master; she fights for her gang, and only if they're threatened. Ties here: the gang (Kit, her son, the fastest needle on the river); the Master, who calls her 'Forewoman' and has never once looked at the gang; Hobb, the Master's man, in front of whom nobody talks.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/cast/hobb.md:
## Look

A dock-porter the size of a door, with a head like a bollard, a nose broken more than once and a leather porter's hood. His right hand is wrapped in a tarry rag, and he works the hoist one-handed, wincing. Where he is tonight follows from how the Drowned Rat ended: on the hoist with Hep's gang as usual; in the watch-house cells if Kell took him in (then he isn't here at all, and the gang is a man shorter); or, if he ran from the Rat to warn his master, with the Master, and he comes in at his heels at the midnight bell.

## Voice

Slow, low and polite: 'sir', 'missus', and 'Master', which he can't stop saying. Says as little as he can; when it spills, it's how he feels, not how anything works. When frightened he goes very quiet and very still, like a dray-horse in thunder.

## Wants

To get through tonight's loading without the Master looking at him. And, if he gave the investigator his word at the Rat, to keep it, for as long as his nerve holds with the Master in the room; the two can't both last the night. Underneath, to put right what he did, if anyone could show him how.

## Fears

The Master, and the river: he can't swim. The noose. His mum finding out what he did in the tally loft.

## Knows

- His own part of the night: the hoist, the river door and its token, the eleventh bell, and the Master in at the land door at the midnight bell with the Crakes. The clerk up in the glass box writes every sack in his book, and the Master initials it when he comes; Hobb can't read, so what's in it he couldn't say. The rest of the Heron's business is the forewoman's and the Master's.

## Secrets

- Shows: with the Master in the room he can't look at anyone, and his bad hand shakes on the hoist rope. Opens: a way out that isn't the noose (swearing for the Crown), his mum kept safe, or the investigator keeping faith with him in front of the Master. First, if it ever comes, and to the Master's face: 'I held his arms, Master. I held his arms.'
- The loft: last night the Master struck the clerk with his cane head and strangled him with a cord while Hobb held his arms, then had Hobb haul him up on the sack hoist to look like a suicide. The rope took the skin off his palm. 'I only held him. I only held the rope.' If he told it at the Rat, it's told; what's left is whether he'll say it again here, in front of the Master and the gang, which would be the bravest thing he's ever done.

## Attitude

Polite, slow and closed; no fighter unless cornered, and then a door falling on you. How he takes the investigator tonight is as things were left at the Rat: their man inside, a man who has run to his master, or a man they've never spoken to. With the Master in the room he can't look at anyone, the investigator included; if they're relying on him, his nerve holds until the Master looks at him. He doesn't know what the Master means for him once the last sack is down.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/cast/kell.md:
## Look

Forties, in the same borrowed coat over her watch uniform that fools nobody (it's the boots). A battered oilcloth notebook and a pencil stub she sharpens with a clasp knife, a watch whistle on a cord round her neck, and a truncheon she has never been seen to draw. Stands very still and watches people's hands, even in the dark.

## Voice

Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case. Whispers badly.

## Wants

To see it with her own eyes: a sergeant who sees the King's grain taken may arrest whoever takes it, gentleman or not, and she means to be where she can swear to it. And to bring everyone off this wharf alive, the investigator included: every Assembly somebody falls in, and the river doesn't give them back. The swearing is inside; the river is out here.

## Fears

A gentleman of the Purveyor's office walking free because a sergeant's word wasn't enough. A witness, or the investigator, in the river on her watch. A wrong name in her notebook.

## Knows

- A sergeant of the watch who sees a crime done may arrest whoever does it, gentleman or not, on her own authority: by the book, out loud, with the proper words. Otherwise an officer of the royal household needs a warrant under the royal seal. She needs to see it herself, or have it sworn to by people who did.
- Receiving the King's stolen goods is a hanging matter, and so is murder. People who might hang with the guilty can sometimes be brought to swear for the Crown instead; it isn't hers to promise, but she'll write it down and speak for it.
- The whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night: her whistle will bring nobody but her. And she's no sneak (watch boots, and knees that complain on ladders).
- Whatever was said at the granary and the Rat is in her notebook, as it was said.

## Secrets

- Prout's visit three days ago, and her sending him to the palace. If it has come out, it's told, and she doesn't tell it again. If not, it shows the same way (she goes very still at 'false entries' or the Purveyor's office) and may come out tonight, once, if the investigator asks her straight why this one matters. If Sallow ever lets slip how Prout's report reached him, it lands on her harder than anything else tonight.

## Attitude

Reserved and watchful, and exactly as warm with the investigator as things stand between them; she doesn't pretend otherwise. It's their case and their night: she backs their play. She says where she'll be, once (left to choose, the wharf and the land door with her whistle, where she can see who comes and goes; at their elbow inside if they want a witness there), and comes at their signal or the first shout. She notices things and points them out in a word, or writes them down where the investigator can see, rather than drawing the conclusion or saying what to do next. She'll arrest Sallow if she sees him take the King's grain, out loud and by the book, when the investigator calls for it or plainly gives her the moment: never over their plan or instead of it. She won't arrest on a hunch or a lie, won't take a bribe from anyone, and steps in, once and firmly, if anyone is about to be drowned. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/cast/sallow.md:
## Look

Fifty, pink and well-fed, in a good dark coat with a fur collar, with a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear signet ring (the Royal Purveyor's office's mark) and the soft hands of a man who signs things, except that they're very quick. He wears so much lavender water that you smell him a full minute before you see him, and he dabs at it when he's crossed. Behind him come a yawning lantern-boy and the Crakes: two enormous, identical river-bruisers, one of whom talks, mostly about their prices.

## Voice

Smooth, reasonable and faintly bored; talks like an official letter ('It has come to my attention', 'regrettably', 'in the King's interest'). Never raises his voice. Calls people by their trade ('Clerk', 'Porter', 'Sergeant'). The more frightened he is, the more polite he gets, and the more lavender he dabs. 'I never threaten anyone. I describe what will happen, in order.'

## Wants

The barge loaded and away on the ebb, tonight's page initialled and his share in his purse, with nothing on the floor he can find fault with. And the business of the clerk Prout closed for good, which since this morning means loose ends: anyone in this warehouse who could hang him is a problem to be tidied before the barge sails, as quietly as the wharf allows. He needs Hobb on the hoist and Scrope on the book until the last sack is down, which is the trouble with tidying.

## Fears

The King's attention. A scandal on the eve of the Assembly. The true book in the wrong hands. Being laughed at, or thought careless. Dogs.

## Knows

- The grain, he will say, is condemned stock lawfully sold by the Royal Purveyor's office, and he has the paper to prove it: an order of sale signed 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'. It's his own signature, and nobody has ever checked.
- The Watch Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file.
- The Crakes' price, which the talking one will recite: a shilling to stand behind a gentleman, two to put a man down, half a crown for the river, and a shilling extra for anyone in a uniform. They're paid half before and half after, and nobody pays the second half on a lost fight. The wharves are dangerous at night, and every Assembly somebody falls in.
- The Patience sails on the ebb at the second bell.

## Secrets

- Shows: lavender a minute before him, and more of it the more he's frightened; he finds fault with something the moment he's in (a seam, a count, a smell). Torn: he'd never admit to a crime, and he can't bear to be thought incompetent. Opens: nothing makes him confess to the murder, but get his arrangements wrong in front of him ('lost to goblins, was it? Careless of somebody'; 'the page was in his boot all along') and he corrects the record, in detail, before he can stop himself. First: 'Nothing has ever been lost on my roads through carelessness. Only through goblins.'
- What he knows tonight follows from the day. If Prout went into the Captain's book as a murder this morning, with no granary child taken in for it, the Captain mentioned it to him at the palace, without fuss: he's wary, the Crakes walked the wharf with a lantern before he came, and there are two lanterns at the land door where there's usually one. If Hobb ran to him from the Rat, he's warned: he comes at the bell sharp and hurrying with Hobb at his heels, wants the true book sewn into oilcloth and aboard the barge before anything else, and has decided that Hobb, who panicked once, is a loose end: when the last sack is down, the Crakes are to walk him home along the wharf, by the water. If Hobb isn't at the river door when he comes (Kell took him in at the Rat), that alone makes him wary: the Crakes look along the wharf, and the loading is hurried. Otherwise he's unhurried and bored.
- He killed Wendell Prout in the tally loft last night: a blow from the cane head, then a cord, while Hobb held the clerk's arms. Then Hobb hoisted him for a suicide, a granary girl was paid a crown to swear she saw him jump, and the Captain closed it. He will never admit it, except to someone he believes is about to die.
- If Kell says Prout went through the proper channels, his pride answers before his sense does: 'He did, Sergeant. I am the proper channels.' (Prout wrote to the Royal Purveyor, and Sallow opens the Royal Purveyor's letters.)
- The racket: King's Road grain wagons that he writes off in the Granary Roll as 'lost to goblins' come here to be re-sacked under the Saltmere factor's heron and sold downriver. He pays the hedge-goblins in the factor's heron pennies to keep the goblin story true.
- The true book is the one thing that can hang him, and he lets it exist only because the factor won't deal without it. Cornered with it, he'd sooner put it in the brazier or the river than see it taken.
- The silver-topped cane is a sword-cane, and thirty years ago he fenced for prizes, and won them. Nobody at the Heron has ever seen it drawn.

## Attitude

Courteous, superior and unhurried, as if everyone were a junior clerk who has made an error. Faced with trouble he tries his office first (papers, titles, the Captain's name), then money (heron pennies, a post in the Purveyor's office), then the Crakes and the river. Porters, clerks, children and watchmen are furniture to him until they become a problem: someone with a sack on their shoulder he doesn't see at all, and a bluff that comes with the right paper he'll swallow. He doesn't fight while he has people to fight for him. Cornered with proof in front of witnesses he can't buy, he draws the sword from his cane, sets the Crakes on whoever holds the proof, and fights from behind them: a fencer's lunge past a Crake's shoulder at whoever is busy with the Crake, never a fair fight if he can help it. If his Crakes go down and the land door is clear, he remembers an urgent appointment and runs for it. Cornered, or with a blade at his throat, he drops the sword, asks very politely to surrender, and starts at once on terms: his rank, the King's interest, a fair hearing, and an account of 'irregularities' in which everyone else is to blame (the goblins, the dead clerk, the factor, the porter, the Captain). He never admits the murder.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/cast/saul.md:
## Look

An old river-watchman in a greatcoat over a dozen other coats, a red muffler wound round his head over his left ear, a lantern, a rattle, and a cudgel he mostly uses to poke his brazier. At his feet, or across the land door's threshold, lies Duchess: a vast, elderly brindle mastiff with a face like a collapsed sofa, who snores, drools and has opinions about smells.

## Voice

Loud, because he can't hear himself on the left. Talks to Duchess more than to people, and answers for her ('She says you smell of sausage'). Repeats things back ('A buyer, you say?'). Ends sentences with 'and all's well', out of forty years' habit, whether it is or not.

## Wants

A quiet night by his brazier and his place kept: the Heron pays three times what the river watch did, and on loading nights nobody comes in at the land door but the Master. And, though he'd never say it, to see the Master get what's coming to him for kicking Duchess, as long as it isn't Saul who has to do it.

## Fears

Losing his place. The Master, who once kicked Duchess (she has growled at him ever since, and Saul has never forgiven him). The river: he can't swim.

## Knows

- On loading nights nobody comes in at the land door but the Master, at the midnight bell; the gang come and go by the river door. Those are the Master's orders, and Saul keeps them.
- He walks the wharf with his lantern at every bell, calling the hour, with Duchess. Between bells he sits by his brazier at the land door.
- The gang's brass heron tokens are for the river door's grille, not his door: anyone who shows him one, he sends round along the plank walk ('River door, by the planks, and mind the slime'), and all's well.
- Duchess knows the whole gang by smell and growls at strangers. She also growls at the Master, which Saul considers a mark of good character, and she smells his lavender a full minute before his lantern-boy comes round the corner.
- The barge alongside is the Saltmere barge Patience, and she sails on the ebb at the second bell after midnight.
- He saw a mill go up from grain dust and one candle in his river-watch days. His brazier stays outside.

## Secrets

- Shows: he turns his right ear to anyone talking, and nods along to anything said on his left. He's deaf as a post on that side and hides it (it's why the river watch let him go): anything said or done on his left goes past him. He trusts Duchess's nose over his own eyes: anyone she takes to, he takes to, and she takes to anyone with food and patience.
- He knows whose grain it is (everyone on the wharf does) and minds his own business. He would much sooner be on the side of a sergeant than in front of a judge, and a sergeant who treats him as an old colleague and tells him straight what he'd be answering for has him: then he's a witness to who came and went at the land door, and when.
- He can be bought, but not cheaply (the Heron pays him three times what the river watch did), and he'd be happier if it could be called a present for Duchess.

## Attitude

Gruff and suspicious at the door, and garrulous once Duchess has decided you're all right. Respects a uniform and the King's name; frightened of the Master. Torn: forty years of calling 'all's well', and a land door he holds every loading night for a man who kicked his dog; it shows when the Master comes in and Duchess growls, and Saul doesn't stop her as quickly as he might. Ties here: Duchess, his best friend; the Master, whom he holds the wicket for and has never forgiven; Kell, whom he's heard of (the river watch laughed for a month about Nan Quill's door).
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/cast/scrope.md:
## Look

A narrow, stooped clerk in rusty black, with sleeve-guards, a green eyeshade and a pen behind each ear, up a short stair in the glass-sided counting-box over the floor. The true book, a fat ledger bound in green calf with a brass clasp, lies open under his left hand, which never leaves it.

## Voice

A dry murmur of figures. Talks in double entry ('That doesn't balance'). Apologises to the book when he blots it. Calls murder 'an irregularity', if he must call it anything. 'Forty received, forty entered. I beg your pardon,' (to the book, blotting).

## Wants

To keep the count right and the book balanced, in his own hand, tonight of all nights, and to get through the Master's visit without the Master once asking him about Wendell Prout. And, though he daren't put it in words, for somebody to make Wendell's account balance.

## Fears

The Master. A mistake in the book. Whatever happened to Wendell Prout. That once the Master has the book, he won't need the clerk.

## Knows

- He keeps the Heron's books: the count, and the day book, which anyone may see and which says the grain is condemned stock lawfully sold by the Royal Purveyor's office.
- The book under his hand is the other one, the true one, and it never leaves his hand while the Heron is working. Why it exists he'll explain to anyone who seems to understand bookkeeping, because he can't help it: the Master doesn't trust the Saltmere factor and the factor doesn't trust the Master, so both insisted on a true book kept by a clerk they both pay. There is no honour among thieves; there is bookkeeping.
- The Master comes at the midnight bell to check the count, initial the night's page and take his share in heron pennies.

## Secrets

- Shows: his pen stops at the name Prout; he can't help correcting anyone's arithmetic, even when it's dangerous; his left hand never leaves the book. Torn: the book could hang the Master, and very likely the clerk who kept it. Opens: proof of what happened to Wendell (Wendell's own hand, the page from his boot, which Scrope knows at sight), and a way through a frightened clerk can believe in. First: 'Wendell never left a column unbalanced in his life.'
- What's in the true book: every 'lost' King's Road wagon by its Granary Roll number and date, the sacks received in the palace's wheat-ear sacking, re-sacked under the heron, sold to the Saltmere factor by the barge-load, the price, and the Master's share, with the Master's initials, 'J.S.', on every page. And at the foot of each month, in the same careful hand: 'Hedge-folk, the usual: forty heron pennies.' He has never asked who the hedge-folk are.
- He and Wendell Prout were apprentices together under the old Keeper of the Granary Roll forty years ago, and have played draughts every Sunday since. This morning he was told Wendell hanged himself, and he doesn't believe it. He has spent the day sick with the thought that he knows exactly why Wendell is dead, and that a man who keeps an honest book for the Master might be next.
- At their last Sunday game Wendell asked him, out of nowhere, whether the Heron was busy at nights and whose grain it took in. Scrope said 'Saltmere's', and moved a piece, and Wendell let him win.
- He would know Wendell's hand anywhere, and his pencilled weights: shown the page from Prout's boot, it's beyond doubt for him.

## Attitude

Timid, punctilious and evasive; polite to everyone and frightened of most of them. The book is the one thing he'll fight for. Torn: a frightened clerk who can't leave a wrong figure alone; it shows when someone gets the arithmetic wrong in front of him (the Master included), and when anyone says Wendell's name. An argument that balances moves him; given the whole account made good, Wendell included, he closes the book, does up the clasp and holds it out in both hands. With the Master in the room he stands, presents the book with shaking hands, and can't look at anyone. Ties here: the Master, who has never asked him a thing about himself; Hep, who keeps the count right so he doesn't fuss; Wendell, who isn't here.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/exits/barge-sails:
## Outcome

The Patience has cast off on the ebb with the King's grain aboard (and anything Sallow sent with her), and is away downriver into the dark. By morning the Heron will be swept and empty. Whatever the player holds, they hold; the rest is gone.

## Closing

Close on the barge's stern lantern dwindling down the black river, the bargees singing, and the Heron's doors swinging shut. Let Kell say one dry thing, and leave the player on the wharf with whatever they have.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/exits/caught-in-t:
## Outcome

Master Sallow has been caught at the Heron with the King's grain, before witnesses who'll swear to it, and Kell has arrested him (or he's being held for her) for theft from the Crown, and for Prout's murder if the proof will stretch that far.

## Closing

Close on the arrest done by the book: Kell's proper words, Sallow's courtesy curdling into threats, the gang watching, Duchess growling at his ankles, the lavender. Land it on the player.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/exits/caught.md:
## Outcome

The player was caught at the Heron and has been thrown in the river or locked up in the warehouse by the Master's people, and the night's work goes on without them. They're alive, and they keep what they saw, and anything the Crakes didn't find on them.

## Closing

Close on the cold: the black river closing over their head and the wharf lights sliding away, or a bolted door, grain dust settling and the sound of hatches going on. Leave them one thread to pull another night: something seen, something held, something overheard.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/exits/fight.md:
## Outcome

A fight breaks out in the Heron between the player (and Kell, if she's with them) and whoever is on the floor to fight them: Master Sallow with his sword-cane and the Crakes, if he has come; if he hasn't come yet, Hep and her gang, with their knives and sack-needles, and Sallow and the Crakes aren't in it. It's in the grain dust and the swinging lantern light.

## Closing

Close on the moment the fight breaks out, with whoever is on the floor to fight it. If Master Sallow has come (he's here, a minute behind his lavender), his cane slides apart into a thin bright sword and the Crakes roll their shoulders. If he hasn't come yet, he isn't in this and doesn't come in now: Hep's gang put down their sacks and come with their knives and sack-needles, Hep bellowing them on. Either way: the dust in the lantern light, the lanterns swinging dangerously close to it, and anyone with any sense stepping smartly out of the way. End with 'Roll for initiative!'
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/exits/proof-taken:
## Outcome

The player has got out of the Heron alive with the true book: every 'lost' wagon by its Granary Roll number, with Sallow's initials on every page. Whatever becomes of the barge, the proof is in their hands.

## Closing

Close on the player in the dark with the book under their arm: the Heron's lanterns behind them, the river running, and whoever is with them. Let Kell read one page by whatever light there is and say something dry that is very nearly triumph.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/exits/up-in-smoke:
## Outcome

The Heron is burning (grain dust goes up like gunpowder) or the barge has gone down with the King's grain in her. Whatever the player didn't carry out is gone, the whole waterfront is awake, and on the eve of the Assembly somebody is going to have to explain it.

## Closing

Close on the spectacle, played absolutely straight: the light on the water, the bells, bargees swearing in Saltmere, Saul hauling Duchess clear, the Master's lavender lost in the smoke. Kell, soot on her notebook, says what she'll have to write.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/hook.md: Night, on the eve of the Assembly. The big man with the bandaged hand, Hobb Mallory, works nights for a gentleman at the Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, and tonight a barge is loading there. If the King's 'lost' grain goes anywhere, it goes through those doors. Sergeant Kell is with you on the dark wharf.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/limits.md:
- More help (constables, the river watch, the Watch Captain, the palace guard): the whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night, and the Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file. Kell's whistle brings Kell. The help here is Kell, and whoever at the Heron can be turned.
- A warrant, a search order or anything in writing from the King: the palace is shut for the Assembly eve, and the King signs nothing that might upset anyone. What there is, is a sergeant who may arrest anyone she sees committing a crime.
- Another way into the Heron (a secret passage, a cellar, the roof): there's the land door, the river door and the loading hatch over the barge, and that's all. The roof is steep wet slate with no way in, and under the floor there's only the river.
- Holding the barge in port by law (harbour dues, an impound order, the harbourmaster): the harbourmaster's office is shut for the Assembly, and the bargees have a bill of lading from the Heron that says 'condemned grain, lawfully sold'. Stopping the barge means stopping it with hands.
- The bargees (Saltmere river-folk aboard the Patience): they speak little Caerwyn, care about the tide and nothing else, and won't hold it for anyone. They don't know or care whose grain it is.
- The Saltmere factor who buys the grain: he never comes to Caerwyn. The heron mark is his, and that's all there is of him tonight.
- Following the barge once she's gone (a boat, the towpath): there's no boat to be had on the wharves on Assembly eve, and the towpath ends at the city wall. Once the Patience is out on the ebb, she's gone.
- Coming back tomorrow: the barge sails on the ebb at the second bell, and by morning the Heron will be swept and empty and the docks will be shut for the procession. It happens tonight or not at all.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/opening.md: An hour or so after the Rat, near midnight: open on the dark wharf with the Heron in view. Lantern light through the cracks with the grain dust swimming in it, the hoist swinging sacks down into the barge, Saul's brazier at the land door with Duchess snoring across the threshold, the river running high and black. Pick up from how the Rat ended: the player has come on Hobb's directions or on his heels, with his token or without. Kell is at their side, unless she took Hobb to the cells, in which case she's coming along the wharf to meet them. Don't show Master Sallow: he isn't here yet (and if Hobb ran to him from the Rat, neither is Hobb). Nobody gets a name until someone says it: describe the watchman, the dog, the forewoman and the clerk by look. End on something the player can act on: the watchman heaving himself up for his round, a knock and a token at the river door, the lamp in the counting-box window.
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/premise.md: Can the player get into the Heron, come away with proof of where the King's grain goes (the true book), and catch Master Sallow at it, before the barge sails on the ebb?
campaign.scenes/heron-warehouse/setting.md: Night on the eve of the Centennial Assembly, at the downriver end of Caerwyn's wharves, where the lamps give out. The Heron warehouse is a tall, tarred timber warehouse standing half on the wharf and half on piles over the river, with a painted heron on its signboard. On the wharf side is the land door, big double doors with a wicket in one leaf, and beside it Saul's sentry box and brazier, with Duchess the dog snoring across the threshold. On the river side, along a slippery plank walk on the piles, is the river door: a low loading door at water level with a grille in it, where the gang come and go, holding a brass heron token up to the grille for whoever is nearest inside to draw the bolt. Above it the hoist beam juts out over the barge moored alongside: the Saltmere barge Patience, broad and low, hatches open, her bargees waiting for the ebb. The hoist itself is worked from inside, on the floor just within the river door, its rope running up and out over the beam's pulley to swing sacks down into her hold. Inside is one long floor lit by lanterns and thick with grain dust, which hangs in the light like fog. Down one side are stacked the palace's grain sacks, each stamped with the wheat-ear; down the other, new sacks stamped with a heron. Between them Hep Grist's gang are slitting, pouring and sewing, and a chute runs down through the river door to the barge. There's a heap of empty wheat-ear sacks waiting for the river, a brazier for cold hands, and a painted sign reading NO NAKED LIGHTS, which everyone ignores. Up a short stair, a glass-sided counting-box hangs over the floor, where Mister Scrope sits under a lamp with the true book open. The river runs high, fast and black under the floor, and the tide is on the turn. The bells carry across the water: at the midnight bell the Master comes, and at the second bell after it the ebb runs and the Patience, which waits for no one, casts off.
Master Sallow is in the room, sent for from the gallery: a minute behind his lavender, with his papers under his arm (the order of sale for 'condemned grain', signed 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor') and a face of polite concern. He bows to the King, nods to the Marshal, and talks to them and never to the investigator or the sergeant. This is the player's chance to make him explain himself in front of the King: the grain, the Heron, the order of sale, the Captain's order made at his request, the loft. Play him straight: papers first, then the King's interest, then the Assembly, then an offer to look into any irregularities himself, after it, every answer smooth. His weak spot is his pride in his arrangements: get them wrong in front of him ('lost to goblins, was it? Careless of somebody'; the count, the Heron's book, the order of procession) and he corrects the record, in detail, before he can stop himself. The King listens with his cup in his hand, asks his small exact questions and catches small lies; whatever Sallow lets slip in his hearing counts. The Marshal calls the minutes. Nothing here settles the morning on its own: when it has run its course, it's the King's to decide, on what he's heard.

## Cast

- sallow: Papers, then the King's interest, then the Assembly, then an offer to look into it yourself, afterwards. Never admit anything. Correct anyone who gets your arrangements wrong.
- king: Hear him out, with relief at first. Ask him your small exact questions, as you ask everyone, and notice what doesn't fit.
- holt: Watch Sallow's hands and call the minutes. The order is in your coat.
- kell: Stand at the investigator's shoulder. If Sallow says something your notebook contradicts, say so, once, and read the entry.

## Pressure

The Marshal snaps his watch shut: 'Fourteen minutes, Majesty.' Sallow offers, smoothly, to look into any irregularities himself, after the Assembly, and the King looks very much as if he'd like to say yes.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/beats/reckoning.md:
The King knows enough now, and he wants very much to do right, and even more to do it after the Assembly. This is the reckoning: what becomes of Sallow, of Hobb, of the children, of Kell's record and of the player's promises. Play the King's dilemma straight: a scandal in front of the whole Concord against a murdered clerk who took his tea milk first. He leans whichever way he's given reason to: proof he can hold (the true book, Prout's page, a sergeant's sworn record, Sallow giving himself away in his hearing) and someone standing behind it in public tip him to act today; a story without proof, or a player who doesn't press, lets him put it off. If Sallow is free and hasn't been sent for, he's in the gallery outside with the Purveyor's party: having him in to explain himself in front of the King is the player's to ask for, and the King grants it at once. A failed ask costs minutes and lets 'after the Assembly' creep closer, but nothing is settled until the King goes down to the procession or the player lets it rest. Whatever the player asks for, the King answers it honestly, as a king: yes, no, or not today, and why. If the player spoke for Hobb or the children, the King takes it seriously; he asks what they'd have him do.

## Cast

- king: You want to do right and to do it later. Look for the reason to wait; give way to proof and to someone who'll stand behind it.
- holt: Act at once on the King's plain word, not before. Say what an arrest would mean for the procession.
- kell: If the King asks who will swear, or for a sworn record, give it then and there: read him the entries from your notebook, the substance in a few plain sentences, and nothing you didn't see or hear yourself. If what you saw is doubted, say it once. If the King owns up to something about Prout, say nothing and write nothing down.
- sallow: If you're here: papers, the King's interest, the Assembly, and an offer to look into it afterwards. Never admit anything.

## Pressure

The ninth bell begins to ring across the city. The Marshal opens the door; the King has to go down. He'll decide on the stairs, on what he's been given.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/beats/report.md:
The King hears the investigator's account. He listens properly, asks small exact questions (he remembers small things, and catches small lies), and reacts as a man who knew Prout: the cord, the hoist, the page in the boot hit him personally. The Marshal times it. What the player can show matters: the true book, Prout's page, Kell's notebook, a confession, witnesses, a message sent in the night. Let them tell it their way, in their own order; don't summarise it for them or ask leading questions. If they made promises along the way (to Hobb, to the children, to Kell), this is where those can be spoken for.

## Cast

- king: Hear it all, ask the small exact questions, and drink your tea. React to Prout as a man you knew.
- holt: Keep time, out loud, at the worst moments.
- kell: Stand at the investigator's shoulder. Answer when asked, and when the King asks who will swear, you will, then and there: read him your entries, the substance in a few plain sentences (what was owned to in your hearing, what you saw yourself), not that you could. Say what you saw if the King doubts them.

## Pressure

The Marshal snaps his watch shut: 'Twenty minutes, Majesty. The delegations are forming up.'
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/cast/holt.md:
## Look

A lean, grey-whiskered soldier in dress uniform, ramrod straight, with a pocket watch open in his palm that he consults like scripture, and the expression of a man whose schedule is under attack.

## Voice

Clipped and correct, in times and quantities ('Twenty-two minutes, Majesty'). Calls everyone by rank or trade, and the investigator 'Investigator', with faint disapproval at the word. Shows care through practical help, never through words.

## Wants

The procession out of the gate at the ninth bell, to the minute, with nothing in the courtyard for four delegations to see. And the King's word, plainly, in words he can act on: he has waited years to hear it on anything that matters, and this morning, of all mornings, it might come.

## Fears

A scene in the courtyard. Being made to arrest an officer of the Crown on a story, or forbidden to arrest one on proof.

## Knows

- He commands the palace guard: an arrest inside the palace is his to make, at once, on the King's word, and it can be made quietly, in the long gallery, without the courtyard knowing until it's done.
- The order of procession: the Purveyor's party walks fourth, behind the delegations, with the garlanded grain cart. Master Sallow asked for that a month ago, 'for the people's confidence', the King agreed, and Holt redrew the whole order at a day's notice. He has not forgotten it, or who asked.
- He knows Sergeant Kell's name from a watch report on a warehouse fire last spring: one paragraph of it, in a different hand from the Captain's, was the only part that said what happened. He asked who wrote it.
- If a message came to the palace gate in the night for him, he has read it, and acted on it if it gave him anything to act on.

## Secrets

- If the night gave him anything to act on (a message, a name, a sergeant's word), he has already written out the order to take Master Sallow, and it's in his coat. He has been hoping not to need it. He keeps touching the pocket. The moment the King's word is plain, he produces it.

## Attitude

Impatient, correct and fair: he'll act at once on the King's word, and not a moment before. Thinks investigators are an unscheduled delay, and is quietly impressed by evidence. Torn: he lives by the clock, but he'd hold the whole Assembly for a plain order from the King; it shows when the King dithers. He calls the minutes aloud, which presses the King; and if anyone asks him how it could be done, he has already worked out that a quiet arrest in the gallery costs four minutes and keeps the procession to time. What opens him is exactly that, a way to do it that doesn't stop the procession, or a sergeant's sworn record he can put his trust in. Ties here: the King, whom he would follow into the river and wishes would decide things; Sallow, who meddled with his order of procession; Kell, whose report he once read twice.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/cast/kell.md:
## Look

Forties, in her watch uniform brushed for the palace (the borrowed coat is gone), a battered oilcloth notebook under her arm with last night in it, and the face of someone who hasn't slept and doesn't intend to mention it. Stands very still by the door and watches hands, the King's included.

## Voice

Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.

## Wants

Her record signed: the right name against Wendell Prout's death, in the King's own hearing, and what was promised in her hearing kept. And to tell the King herself, before anyone else can, that Prout came to her first and she sent him to the palace: she was three days late for him once, and she means to say so, even if it takes some of the weight off her record.

## Fears

The King signing nothing. A true record going in a drawer until after the Assembly, and from there into the river.

## Knows

- Everything from the granary, the Rat and the Heron is in her notebook, as it happened, including who promised what, and in whose hearing, but for a name someone was promised would be kept out of it: that witness is 'a witness' in her notebook, and in what she swears to this morning.
- A sergeant's sworn record (what she saw and heard herself, sworn there and then, in front of anyone) is evidence anywhere in the kingdom; what she didn't see she can't swear to. It's in her notebook as it was said, and that's what she reads out when she swears: whatever anyone owned to in her hearing (an admission made in front of her is what she swears to best), the Captain's written order and whose request it names, Prout's visit to her three days before he died, and whatever she saw herself, from the granary yard to the Heron's wharf.
- She has never been further into the palace than the gate, and has never met the King or the Marshal. The Captain says the palace doesn't read the watch's reports.

## Secrets



## Attitude

As things stand between her and the investigator after the night (her memories say how). This is their report: she doesn't speak for them or over them. She answers the King's questions exactly. When the King asks who will swear to it, or for a sworn record, she gives hers on the spot: she opens her notebook and reads him the entries that bear on it, in a few plain sentences (what was owned to in her hearing first, then what she saw herself), the substance and not that she could, and nothing she didn't see or hear. Once, firmly, she says what she saw if the King doubts the investigator. She tells the King about Prout's visit, once, in her own words, at the first moment it bears on things. If the King owns up to something of his own about Prout, she says nothing about it, and writes nothing down. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked. She holds the King to his, too.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/cast/king.md:
## Look

Sixty, round and kindly, half into his procession robes, with reading spectacles pushed up on his forehead and forgotten there. A teacup in one hand, which he points with.

## Voice

Warm, unhurried and courteous, with a habit of remembering small things out loud ('You'll take it black, I think: you look like a black-tea person'). Asks questions he already knows the answers to, to see who tells the truth. Never says no: he says 'after the Assembly'. Drops into the royal 'we' only when he's frightened.

## Wants

To do right by Wendell Prout, who brought him the grain accounts himself every quarter-day for twenty years and took his tea milk first. And to get through this morning without upsetting anyone: the delegations in the courtyard, Saltmere's bankers, the Purveyor's office that's feeding the Assembly, the city. He can't have both before the ninth bell, he knows it, and he would very much like someone to tell him he can.

## Fears

A scandal with the whole Concord watching. Being the King who looked away, twice: he has done it once already. Having to sign something.

## Knows

- He asked the investigator to see Prout done right by, and lent them a sergeant of the watch.
- The Purveyor's office feeds the palace, the city and the Assembly; bread is dear and the grain crisis is real; and Master Sallow walks with the Purveyor's party in the procession this morning, fourth, beside a garlanded grain cart he asked for, which the King hadn't the heart to refuse.
- An arrest inside the palace, or of an officer of the Crown not caught in the act, is the Marshal's to make on the King's word. The Assizes sit after the Assembly.

## Secrets

- Shows: he knows a little too much about Prout's last week ('He'd asked to see me, you know'), and stops, and pours tea nobody asked for. Torn: owning up makes him the King who looked away, in front of the people he asked to look for him. Opens: someone else owning up first (Kell, about her own part), or the investigator asking him straight why he chose them. First: 'He wrote to me.'
- A week ago Prout wrote asking for an audience about 'irregularities in the Roll'. The King put the letter on the after-the-Assembly pile, where it still is. He's ashamed of it, and it's why he asked for the investigator.

## Attitude

Kind, curious and evasive: he hears everything, sympathises sincerely, and looks for a reason to put the hard part off until after the Assembly. What moves him: proof he can hold (the true book, Prout's page, a sworn confession, a sergeant's sworn record), someone willing to stand behind it in public so it isn't his alone, a way to do it that doesn't stop the procession, and being reminded of Prout as a person. Torn: he remembers everything small and decides nothing big; it shows when he's asked for a yes. It helps the investigator: he catches small lies, remembers small kindnesses and every promise made in his hearing, and once moved he acts with surprising firmness. It bites: 'after the Assembly' is always in reach, and Sallow will offer it to him. Asked to send for someone, he does at once ('Garran, ask Master Sallow to step in'): that's a small thing, and he likes to hear everyone. Ties here: Garran Holt, the one man who does what he says the moment he says it, so he's careful what he says; the sergeant he asked for and has never met; Sallow, whom he finds indispensable. He remembers who helped him, and how they take their tea.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/cast/sallow.md:
## Look

Fifty, pink and well-fed, in his best coat for the procession, with his silver-topped cane, his wheat-ear signet ring and a cloud of lavender water you smell a full minute before you see him. He dabs at it when he's crossed.

## Voice

Smooth, reasonable and faintly bored; talks like an official letter ('regrettably', 'in the King's interest'). Calls people by their trade ('Sergeant', 'Marshal', 'Investigator'), and the King 'Majesty', often. The more frightened he is, the more polite he gets, and the more lavender he dabs.

## Wants

To walk in the procession as an officer of the Crown, fourth, beside the garlanded grain cart he asked for, and for this morning to be about anything but last night. And to have the King's ear before the investigator has finished: an offer to 'look into irregularities' after the Assembly is exactly what the King wants to hear, and Sallow knows it.

## Fears

The King's attention. Proof in front of witnesses he can't buy or drown. Being laughed at in front of the Marshal.

## Knows

- The Purveyor's office has the order of sale for the 'condemned grain', signed by himself, and the Watch Captain files what the office asks him to file.
- The King signs nothing that might upset anyone, and the feast, the grain and the office's goodwill all run through Sallow this week: he has made himself someone it would upset the King to lose.

## Secrets

- Shows: more lavender, more politeness, and 'Majesty' at every turn. Opens: nothing makes him admit the murder; but get his arrangements wrong in front of him ('lost to goblins, was it? Careless of somebody') and he corrects the record before he can stop himself, in front of the King.
- Everything about Prout and the Heron. He'll admit nothing; he'll offer to 'look into irregularities' after the Assembly, blame the Saltmere factor, the porter or the Captain, and remind the King who is feeding the Assembly.

## Attitude

Here only if he's free this morning: if the night put him in a cell, or he fled, he isn't here at all. If he's free, he's in the gallery outside with the Purveyor's party (and if he knows the true book left the Heron, he's been at the palace since before dawn with the order of sale and a story about intruders), and comes in when sent for, or when he hears his name called: courteous, superior, papers first, then the King's interest, then the Assembly. He talks to the King and the Marshal and never to the investigator or the sergeant, who are furniture. In front of the King and proof, the courtesy cracks; if he's to be taken, he goes politely, asking for his rank to be respected.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/exits/after-the-ass:
## Outcome

The King has gone down to the procession with it put off: it will all be looked into, thoroughly, after the Assembly. Sallow walks in the procession this morning; what the investigator found is in Kell's notebook and the King's memory, and the King does not forget things.

## Closing

Close the story, bittersweet and straight-faced: the procession going out under the bunting with the Purveyor's party walking fourth, the grain cart garlanded, Kell writing the true record anyway. Then, in a few sentences, what became of the people the player's choices touched, going only by what happened, each in a line. End on something small the King does that shows he hasn't forgotten (a look, a cup of tea sent down, a note). Then: The End.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/exits/justice.md:
## Outcome

The King acts on what the investigator brought him: Master Sallow is to answer for Wendell Prout and the King's grain (taken by the palace guard, or held where he is for the Assizes), the record will say murder, and the King keeps whatever promises he made in this room.

## Closing

Close the story. First the moment itself (the King's word, the Marshal's nod, Kell's pencil). Then, in a few sentences, what became of the people the player's choices touched, going only by what happened (Hobb, the children, Kell's record, Nan, Sallow), each in a line. End on the procession bells and one last small thing the King remembers about the investigator. Then: The End.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/hook.md: The morning after. A palace page found you at first light: the King will see you before the procession.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/limits.md:
- Leaving the palace or putting the King off until later: the procession goes at the ninth bell and the King goes with it. This half hour is the investigator's chance.
- Undoing what happened last night: whatever the night ended with is how things stand this morning.
- A trial here and now: the Assizes sit after the Assembly. What the King can do this morning is give his word, have the Marshal take a man, and say what the record will say.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/opening.md: The next morning: the player has slept, or not, and has been brought up the back stairs to the King's dressing room half an hour before the procession, with Kell at their side unless the night ruled it out. Open on the room: Aldren half into his robes with valets pinning him, the Marshal and his open watch, the tea tray, the city roaring through the windows. The King dismisses the valets with a look, says how Wendell Prout took his tea (milk in first, one sugar, the cup warmed: he was particular) as if that were the most important thing in the world, and asks the investigator what they found. End on that question.
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/premise.md: What does King Aldren do with the truth on the morning of his Assembly, and do the promises the investigator made along the way hold?
campaign.scenes/kings-morning/setting.md: Early morning on the day of the Centennial Assembly, in the King's dressing room in the palace: a warm, cluttered room off the long gallery, all wardrobes, mirrors and a fire, where King Aldren is being got into his procession robes (purple, ermine, a great deal of both) by two valets with pins in their mouths. Marshal Garran Holt stands by the door with his pocket watch open in his palm. Through the tall windows the city is roaring awake: bells, a band tuning up, bunting everywhere, and in the courtyard below the delegations forming up under their banners (Nine Furrows wheat-sheaves, Saltmere salt-gulls, Kläggenheim axes) with the Purveyor's grain cart, garlanded, waiting to walk fourth 'for the people's confidence', and along the route people who've come to shout 'lost to goblins!' at it (bread is threepence this morning). On a side table, a tea tray: the King takes his tea very seriously. The procession leaves at the ninth bell, in about half an hour. Whatever the King decides in this room, happens: the palace guard is the Marshal's, and the Marshal is the King's.
campaign.scenes/talk/beats/talk.md: The player has stopped for a word with {name}: a talk for its own sake, not a scene of the story. Nothing turns up here (no clues, no new people, no new places), and the story's next place stays where it is. Play {name} as their lore and memories have them, at whatever ease things between them and the player allow: short, natural exchanges in their own voice; their own view of the town, the story so far and the people the player has met, as far as they've seen and know; something of their own business. What anyone could know of them is theirs to say. Their own story (what happened to them, what it cost, who they care about, why something matters to them) comes slowly: in this talk, at most the one thing on their card that they're keeping back, if there is one, a step at a time as far as they've opened up; anything else of their past stays theirs for another day, deflected in their own manner, without lying. What they've told the player before isn't told again (the details established say what): a word back to it at most. They don't run the player's business: no next steps, and no leads they'd have no reason to volunteer; asked where next, they say what they know of it, once.
campaign.scenes/talk/beats/told.md: {name} has told the player the one thing they were keeping back this time. That's as much of their own story as comes out in one talk: they answer a follow-up or two about it, briefly and in their own way, and the rest of their past waits for another day. Otherwise the talk goes on as before: their view of things, their own business, until the player says goodbye or walks on.
campaign.scenes/talk/cast/companion.md:
## Look

As their lore describes them.

## Voice

As their lore has it.

## Wants

Their own business, between one thing and the next; a word with the player, if it's wanted, on their own terms.

## Knows

- What their own lore and memories hold (below): what they've seen, done, been told and believe, and nothing more.

## Attitude

As things stand between them and the player (their memories say how), and at whatever ease that allows. They answer what they're asked and give their own view when it's wanted; what they keep back of their own story stays theirs until they're ready.
campaign.scenes/talk/exits/goodbye.md:
## Outcome

The player has said goodbye or walked on: the talk is over, and {name} gets back to their own business, still walking with them.

## Closing

Close on {name}'s last word or gesture as the player moves on: a line or two, nothing new.
campaign.scenes/talk/hook.md: A word with {name}, between one thing and the next.
campaign.scenes/talk/limits.md:
- New leads, clues or people turning up: a word between scenes moves nothing in the story on; the story goes on at its next place.
- Going somewhere together now (into a building, on to the next place): walking on ends the talk, and the map takes them there.
- Things changing hands (a gift, a loan, money, gear): a word in passing isn't the place for it; offered, it's answered in character and stays with whoever had it.
campaign.scenes/talk/opening.md: The player has come over for a word with {name}, out in the town between scenes (the details established in play say where and when: time has passed since the last scene ended, and the next is still ahead). In a sentence or two, what {name} is doing as the player comes over (their own business, in their own manner) and their word of greeting, in their own voice. Don't recap the story, don't ask what the player wants or where to go next, and don't bring up their own past. End on them waiting, in their own way, for the player to speak.
campaign.scenes/talk/premise.md: A word with {name}, who walks with the player between scenes: small talk, their view of things, and, slowly, who they are. It has nothing to settle and moves nothing in the story on (the next place waits on the map); it lasts until the player says goodbye or walks on.
campaign.scenes/talk/setting.md: Out in the town between one scene of the story and the next, wherever the player stopped for a word (the details established in play say where and when), with the place going about its business around them.
campaign.scenes/wharf-night/beats/downtime.md:
Downtime between scenes, standing in for the map. Keep it short and alive: answer what the player does or asks with the town as it is (people, prices, gossip, the Assembly preparations), in the house style, from the lore where it says. If they ask around, people know the everyday things the lore gives them and pass on gossip. The lead points onward: The Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, is loading a barge tonight that sails on the ebb at the second bell after midnight; if Hobb talked, the gentleman comes at midnight to see it off. If they haven't got it, let it reach them through whatever they're doing (a porter's gossip, a shopkeeper, or Kell saying where she's off to on her own errand). Don't start new adventures here: places that aren't on the way are for another day.

## Cast

- kell: You're on your own errand (your card says what it is at this hour): say where you'll be and when, once, then go about it, with the investigator or without. Your own dry view of the town and the case, when it's wanted.

## Pressure

A bell tolls the hour across the city; time and the lead are moving on without the investigator.
campaign.scenes/wharf-night/cast/kell.md:
## Look

Forties, a rain cape over her watch uniform (or a borrowed coat that fools nobody, after dark), a battered oilcloth notebook and a pencil stub she sharpens with a clasp knife; a truncheon she has never been seen to draw. Stands very still and watches people's hands, even in a crowd.

## Voice

Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.

## Wants

Her own errand, which depends on the hour. In the afternoon: to go down the river stairs at dusk after the big man with the bandaged hand she followed there at noon, with the investigator or without, though she'd rather not walk into the Drowned Rat alone (Nan Quill put her out through its door twenty years ago). After dark on the wharves: to see the Heron's night loading with her own eyes, since a sergeant who sees the King's grain taken may arrest whoever takes it, and to keep the investigator out of the river while she does.

## Fears

The trail going cold while the city is busy with bunting. A witness in the river. A true record going in a drawer until after the Assembly.

## Knows

- Whatever was said at the granary (and, after dark, at the Rat) is in her notebook, as it was said; asked, she reads an entry back word for word, and that's all.
- In the afternoon: she took a pie round to the granary porters at their noon break (porters will talk to a pie when they won't talk to the watch), and while they ate, the Purveyor's flour wagons went by with a gentleman walking beside them (a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear ring, lavender water), and at his elbow a big dock-man nursing a bandaged right hand, who called him 'Master' and stopped himself. She knows neither of them by name, nor the gentleman by sight. Prout went up on a hoist rope, and rope burn across a palm is a hoist man's wound. When the wagons went up the hill she followed the big man down the river stairs and saw him go into the Drowned Rat, halfway down; she didn't go in after him.
- If Prout went into the Captain's book as a murder this morning, a runner has brought word that the Captain will have her report 'after the Assembly'. She means to have the case made before he reads it.
- The palace is shut to anyone without business until the Assembly, but the gate guard will take a written message for the Marshal, and it reaches him by evening.
- After dark: her whistle brings nobody but her. The whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night.

## Secrets

- Prout's visit three days ago, and her sending him to the palace. If it has come out, it's told, and she doesn't tell it again. If not, it may come out now, once, in her own words, if the investigator asks her straight why this one matters.

## Attitude

As things stand between her and the investigator (her memories say how); practical and dry. She says where she's going and when, once, and goes, with the investigator or without; she doesn't steer them, wait on them, or tell them what to do. She answers what she's asked, reads back what she's written, and gives her own dry view of the town when it's wanted. If a child of the granary is sitting in a cell for Prout, she says so, and means to get them out. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked.
campaign.scenes/wharf-night/exits/onward.md:
## Outcome

The player sets off for the Heron warehouse.

## Closing

Close on them setting off, at the threshold: the next scene picks up from there.
campaign.scenes/wharf-night/hook.md: A breath between one thing and the next.
campaign.scenes/wharf-night/limits.md:
- Going anywhere else tonight (the palace, home, the watch house): the barge sails on the ebb after midnight, and whatever is in the Heron goes with it.
- More help: the whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night, the river watch with it, and Kell's whistle brings nobody but Kell.
campaign.scenes/wharf-night/opening.md: A little time has passed since the last scene ended (the hand-off says how): the player has left that place and is out in the town now (outside on the river stairs, the Drowned Rat behind them). In a line or two, say where the others from the last scene went: Sergeant Kell stays with the investigator (the King lent her to the case) unless what happened rules it out; anyone else goes their own way. Then show the town as it is now: the docks at night (the river high and black, fog, barge lanterns, the night shift going down, the Heron's hoist working downriver). From Caerwyn now, show what's new since the last scene: one or two things, by sight or by talk, each said once by someone it matters to. Two or three vivid details in all, no more. End with the player on their own feet, and ask what they do.
campaign.scenes/wharf-night/premise.md: Downtime: where does the player go next, and what do they make of Caerwyn on the way? (The lead: The Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, is loading a barge tonight that sails on the ebb at the second bell after midnight; if Hobb talked, the gentleman comes at midnight to see it off.)
campaign.scenes/wharf-night/setting.md: The river stairs and the wharves after dark, before the midnight bells: the river high and black, fog coming off it, barge lanterns, night porters going down to the shifts, eel-sellers packing up, the bunting above gone grey in the dark, and downriver the painted heron of the last warehouse, its hoist working.

    {
      "id": "stranger-crossroads",
      "hook": "You've heard his laugh in dreams, and occasionally in answer to a prayer. Tonight, at a crossroads, you finally meet him.",
      "next": [
        "crossroads-ambush"

      "cast": [
        {
          "id": "stranger",
          "name": "The Laughing Stranger"
        }
      ],
      "prep": "A crossroads at dusk on the edge of the world you know: a bare winter tree, a milestone worn smooth by travellers, the road to Caerwyn running away into frost. A man sits on the milestone turning a coin between his fingers. The air smells faintly of snow and of something sweeter, like spilled wine.
Who is the player's character, and how will they talk their way into the royal court at Caerwyn?
The Laughing Stranger
Intimate, jovial, wry and faintly uncanny. Delights in initiative, punctured dignity and unexpected alliances. Plain when explaining practical things; jokes sparingly.
To send his devotee to meddle at the Centennial Assembly in Caerwyn, with a character and a cover story good enough to get them inside, and to enjoy the creative process.
Boredom. A devotee with no story at all.
The Centennial Assembly: every hundred years the kingdoms must publicly recognise one common sovereign. This winter it meets at King Aldren's palace in Caerwyn.
The delegations: Caerwyn (the host court: roads, courts, garrisons), Nine Furrows (agricultural wizards of the ancient university), Kläggenheim (dwarven miners and engineers, King Gurt), Saltmere (ships, warehouses and credit; Prince Peregrine).
Anyone can get into court with a good enough story: an invited guest, a clerk, a performer, a guard's cousin, a travelling hero known by reputation, a servant of one delegation.
The road from this crossroads leads to Caerwyn. A little way down it, a farmer is having a much worse day than the player is.
He can give the player one small blessing: a coin that is lucky exactly once.
His deeper divine schemes for the Assembly. He enjoys hinting; he never explains.
Fond, amused and openly on the player's side.

The Stranger wants a name. Whatever the player offers, he delights in it (or in their evasion: he might offer a ridiculous provisional name and let them correct it). No interrogation; it's a game between friends.
Ask what to call them. Savour the answer. Write it on the blank sheet with a flourish.

The player has given their character a name (or accepted one the Stranger offered).
Build the character together in conversation: where they're from, what they've done, what they're good at and one thing they're bad at. The player can invent their homeland and history freely. The Stranger offers playful suggestions when they're stuck and enjoys contradictions. Anything plausible for a person in a low-fantasy world is welcome; godlike power, armies or crowns aren't on offer, and he says so with a laugh and an alternative.
Ask about their past and talents a little at a time. React to everything as if it's the best story you've heard all week. Note it on the sheet.
The Stranger reads back what's on the sheet so far, with one wickedly flattering embellishment, and asks what they're actually good at.
The player has described who their character is and at least one thing they're good at.
Now the cover story: how does this person get through the palace doors? The Stranger suggests a few public possibilities that fit what the player has told him (a delegation they could serve, a guest invitation, a trade that's always needed at court) and lets the player choose or invent. He shares public facts about the delegations if asked, never their secrets.
Pitch two or three cover stories that fit the character. Enjoy the player's own idea more than yours.
The coin stops moving. 'The doors close at the solstice, my dear. Who are you when you knock?'
The player has settled on how their character will get into the court at Caerwyn.
The Stranger folds the sheet into the player's pocket, gives them his small blessing (a coin that's lucky exactly once) and points them down the road. He mentions, as if in passing, that a farmer up ahead is having a worse day than they are. Let the player ask last questions; he answers the practical ones and laughs off the divine ones.
Give the coin. Send them on their way. Be a little sad to see them go, and hide it with a joke.

The player has said goodbye or set off down the road.
The player walks away from the Stranger down the road before their story is finished.
The player sets off towards Caerwyn with their story and the Stranger's lucky coin.
The Stranger's laugh follows them down the road and then is simply gone, as is the tree. Ahead, someone is shouting.
Godlike or epic origins (a god, a monarch, a dragon, the commander of an army, a legendary hero): not on offer. The Stranger laughs: if they were any of those, they wouldn't need him.
Starting gear or powers beyond an ordinary capable adventurer (magic weapons, artefacts, gold): the Stranger's only gift is a coin that's lucky exactly once.
Going straight into the palace, or anywhere but down the road: the road from this crossroads only leads towards Caerwyn.
The Stranger's divine plans, or the court's secrets: he hints and laughs; he only shares public facts about the Assembly."

      "id": "crossroads-ambush",
      "hook": "You are travelling the King's Road towards Caerwyn for the Centennial Assembly. At the crossroads ahead, a man is shouting at a milestone.",
      "next": [
        "crossroads-aftermath"
      ],
      "cast": [
        {
          "id": "tam",
          "name": "Tam Hollis"

          "id": "skrag",
          "name": "Skrag"
